Connecticut is well represented in Time's inaugural "100 Most Influential Creators" list.
A month after being featured in Forbes' 2025 Top Creators list, Norwalk native Charli D'Amelio was named among the "Titans" of Time's 2025 creators list.

Article continues below this ad
"A pioneer of TikTok fame, Charli D’Amelio’s ascent to social media superstardom began in 2019 when she was just 15 years old. By the end of 2020, her viral dancing and lip-syncing videos had made her the first creator to surpass both 50 million and 100 million TikTok followers," reads Time's description of D'Amelio. "Today, with more than 156 million followers, the 21-year-old is the second-most popular person on the platform."
D'Amelio has expanded her presence outside of social media, lending her voice to the animated feature film "StarDog and TurboCat," making her Broadway debut in "& Juliet" and winning her season of "Dancing With The Stars."
In January, the D'Amelio family sold their South Norwalk condo for $1.825 million and moved to Los Angeles.

To come up with its list, Time looked at top creators on various platforms like YouTube, Twitch, Instagram and TikTok, and "selected those who built careers for themselves natively through these digital platforms," according to Time's website. Time consulted with correspondents, editors and contributors as well as its data and insights partner #paid, a creator marketplace, in order to analyze reach and engagement of those selected.
Also making the list are a handful of notable alumni of Connecticut colleges.

Quinnipiac University alum and Olympian Ilona Maher made the list under the "Phenoms" category. The rugby star has also gone on to star in "Dancing With The Stars" as well as start her own podcast, "House of Maher," and been featured in Sports Illustrated Swimsuit.
Ghanaian-American doctor Joel Bervell, who is known online as the "medical mythbuster," is a 2017 graduate of Yale University. He is a Peabody Award winner who tackles the issues of "racial and gender bias on health care and debunks health misinformation that can harm marginalized communities."
Another Yale graduate featured on the list is Kahlil Greene, who once served as the university's first-ever Black student body president. An Emmy-nominated and Peabody Award-winning educator known as the "Gen-Z historian," Greene has his "History Can’t Hide" Substack newsletter, a National Geographic docuseries that premiered this year and a book deal with Random House Publishing Group.

Not everyone gets to say that they danced alongside BLACKPINK’s Lisa. But then again, online sensation Niana Guerrero isn’t just anybody.
In a short TikTok from March, the two perform “FVCK UP THE WORLD” with the synchronicity and familiarity of long-time teammates. “But I remember telling her before we started that I was so nervous, and she had told me that she was nervous too. Imagine that!” Guerrero tells Teen Vogue over Zoom. It’s not her first celebrity collaboration — far from it, actually. In the past year alone, she’s been spotted with KATSEYE, Meghan Trainor, and Tate McRae. Nevertheless, she still gets the same onslaught of comments with each video drop: “How do I be you? You’re so lucky!”
To chalk it all up to luck, however, would be a disservice to the 19-year-old dancing queen. Guerrero is currently the Philippines’ most-followed TikTok creator with over 45 million followers (and around a billion likes). Her virality extends to YouTube, where an audience of almost 16 million subscribers has watched her grow up.
The most chronically online among us might recognize Guerrero as the baby girl bopping along to “Despacito,” while her older brother Ranz Kyle drove her to an undisclosed location. Running a little past a minute long, it soon spawned a dance craze in the same vein as the Harlem Shake and landed the sibling duo a slot in the 2017 YouTube Rewind, an annual video series featuring the hottest trendmakers of the past year.
Born to a family that valued and nurtured talents in the arts, Guerrero was a shy kid in Manila who turned to movement as a means of self-expression. Her earliest home videos show her trying to imitate Michael Jackson’s distinct dance routines. Behind the camera was her brother, who already had a past life as a member of the Filipino boy band Chicser. (Guerrero’s debut video appearance was actually in their 2011 cover of “Teach Me How to Dougie.”)
Kyle found something special and funny in his little sister’s innate talent, and he began featuring her in his videos as he made the jump to vlogging. Post-”Despacito,” Guerrero’s parents decided to homeschool her. “Initially, I really didn’t think about the views, followers, likes, or anything. I wanted to share my love for dance and show our family spending time together,” Guerrero says.
The pandemic marked yet another turning point in Guerrero’s burgeoning career: like the rest of us, she was grooving to “Say So” and “Supalonely,” but in a more capable fashion. Her feel-good trendsetting content soon introduced her to a new audience in search of light in dark times. Guerrero says that many of her most-replicated dance challenges, like “Booty Wurk,” and “Give It Up,” come from just surrendering to a beat that takes over her body. “Surprisingly, my dance trends that go viral are the ones that just come out of nowhere: I’d be playing the song in my room and then all of a sudden, a choreography would come to mind,” she says. “I’d upload it and then be totally shocked the next day that so many people decided to try it too.
Similarly, the vlogs she posts to her channel of 15 million subscribers don’t follow any specific formula. She gravitates towards content of her parents and siblings bonding together, which resonates with her family-centric Filipino audience — even as they’re ignoring their baby sister Natalia or turning Ranz’s room into a ball pit as a prank.
It was only a matter of time before this effortless authenticity attracted some of her favorite artists. While some collaborations are business deals with terms that are negotiated from the start, many of these interactions started with them sliding directly into Guerrero’s DMs and building a foundation of friendship. It’s safe to say, though, that no moment beats getting noticed by her long-time celebrity crush.
“When Jungkook followed me, I started jumping in my room because I couldn’t believe that it was true,” she says with infectious enthusiasm about BTS’s youngest member. “I even messaged him and said, ‘Oh my god, is this true?’ and when he replied with ‘Yes!’, I freaked out again.”
Last February, yet another BTS member took notice of Guerrero: J-hope both followed and shot her a message, asking if she could teach him how to use TikTok. (The two mutuals even met up during his recently concluded Hope On The Stage Manila leg.) “I was literally in the car on the way to an event when I saw it through a tweet, and I had to check if it was real multiple times because I couldn’t believe it at all,” she says. “BTS is the best K-pop group ever to me.”
Among her other admirers and past collaborators include NCT Dream, Sabrina Carpenter, and even Chef Gordon Ramsay, whom she was “honestly terrified” of back in childhood. (“He’s way nicer than we all think,” she says.) I ask her lightheartedly if she’s going to take this as her first foray into food, which makes her break into a laugh. Probably not, but she’s very willing to explore other fields.
As avid viewers of her livestreams would know, Guerrero has always dabbled in music. It was once an annual tradition for her to collaborate with Ranz on songs centered around the same message of positivity and empowerment. But now, she’s eager to discover what other genres she could pursue.
Current collaborations with Louis Vuitton and BYS Cosmetics also point to her growing influence in the world of fashion and beauty: “I’m trying to be more intentional with the way I present myself, so I’m experimenting a lot right now,” she says. “I’m taking a lot of inspiration from what I see on Pinterest and TikTok and trying to inject my own flavor based on what I’m comfortable with.” We get a sense of her eclectic sensibilities on her Instagram: one day, she’s Cupid in a crimson bodysuit with an accent belt, only for her to dress down into her signature statement tee and sneakers the next.
Unlike her approach to dance, Guerrero’s outlook towards life is less based on vibes. “I think it’s important to go with the flow but I do appreciate structure. I’ll let things happen in a natural way but when it comes to choosing which people to keep in my immediate circle, carving out a space I can be comfortable in, making my own schedule, and having a say in my recent projects, I want to be more conscious now.”
Influencers may find it hard to strike a balance between the personal and public-facing, especially when every moment can be monetized. But Guerrero has never felt the need to follow any trends, or cave to the demands of the majority. “I think it’s easy to get caught up in what people expect of me, but in the end, I always do what feels right for me,” she says. “I want to stay true to who I am.”
Even though her career is pretty much in full force, Guerrero has no plans of letting her personal goals take the backseat. Some of the items on her bucket list for the year? Going to Coachella; exploring Paris; and meeting the likes of Tyla and Jungkook.
Of course, as someone who grew up in the public eye, she also strives to attain simple joys, such as traveling with her close group of friends. “I never got to have sleepovers growing up, so when my friends and I went to Japan and stayed in the same Airbnb, it was the closest I had ever gotten to that experience,” she says. “I loved shopping the whole day and getting home and doing little hauls with them. It was so memorable for me.”
I ask her if there’s anything jarring about having the entire archive of her life available online for public viewing, but she’s never seen it that way.
“I’m grateful that people have seen different versions of me over the years,” Niana Guerrero says. “And though my interests and style and mindset will evolve, I’ll grow and document as I go.”

Vanessa Lopes Ramalho[1] (born July 5, 2001)[2] is a Brazilian digital influencer and dancer, known for having more than 30.5 million followers on TikTok, where she is successful with her choreographies.[3][4] In 2024, she was a participant in the twenty-fourth edition of the reality show Big Brother Brasil; Vanessa's participation was brief and generated controversy.[5][6]
Biography
[edit]Lopes was born in Brasília, but moved to Recife as a child. She created a TikTok account while she was at university and, during the COVID-19 pandemic, started recording and posting dance videos on the app. As of January 2024, Lopes has 30.2 million followers on TikTok and 14.3 million followers on Instagram. She presents the podcast Não é TPM with Fernanda Schneider, Gabriela Mag, Victória Collen, Isa Paoli and Vivi Wanderley.[7][8]
In 2024, Vanessa Lopes was a member of the "Celebrity" group in the 24th season of Big Brother Brasil. In January of the same year, her TikTok account had a total of 1 billion likes.[9][10]
Personal life
[edit]Relationships and personal interests
[edit]Vanessa Lopes is openly bisexual.[11][12] In June 2021, she began dating football player and TikToker Ricardo Rêgo, which lasted six months. Vanessa also had involvement with actor João Guilherme,[13] and publicly shared interactions with other personalities, such as Luísa Sonza,[14] Lara Silva, Gabi Lopes and Gabriel Medina.[15][16]
On social media, Lopes also highlights her passion for sports, being a Flamengo[17][18] fan and a footvolley player,[19] as well as demonstrating an interest in surfing, an activity she also does during her free time.[20]
Accident
[edit]After completing high school, Lopes had the desire to go on exchange and study abroad. However, during a trip with a friend, DJ Alan Maciel, she was hit by a driver who fled the scene, near Porto de Galinhas. They were on their way to a show when their vehicle had a flat tire. At the time of the exchange, a car hit them and threw them about 20 meters away. Vanessa was holding the flashlight so that Maciel could have a better view when changing the tire.[21] At the time of the accident, Vanessa was just 18 years old, and this traumatic experience made her rethink the idea of living far from family and friends, leading her to conclude that it wasn't worth going abroad.[22]
A year after the road tragedy, Lopes decided to split her time between attending college for marketing and getting involved in creating digital content.[23]
Mental health
[edit]Throughout her participation in BBB 24, Lopes revealed that she was confronting emotional triggers from past traumas, showing signs of psychological instability. Her instability increased when comments appeared alleging that she was a superficial person, constantly looking in the mirror, and that her attitudes, including her moments of crying, were not genuine.[24] When faced with the accusations, Vanessa remembered difficult situations she had faced before the reality show, clarifying that her habit of looking in the mirror was a strategy to deal with the temporomandibular disorder she faces and that she seeks to recover.[25] In the following days, her emotional instability intensified, reflected in her increasingly weakened participation. Vanessa also revealed that she felt persecuted, even thinking that she was being persecuted and affected on purpose.[26][27] Furthermore, she made frequent references to George Orwell's book 1984, which inspired the creation of Big Brother.[28] In a peculiar moment, she questioned whether her confinement colleagues were actors, highlighting the depth of her psychological discomfort during the program.[29] Vanessa also got involved in intriguing situations with other participants and even threw away all her colleagues' toothbrushes while cleaning the bathroom.[30][31]
Vanessa's behaviors raised concerns among viewers, who expressed fears about her mental health, urging the show's production team to intervene.[32] There was also speculation about the possibility of a psychotic break during the events.[33] On social media, personalities such as Bruna Marquezine, Jojo Todynho, Mel Maia and Deborah Secco also expressed concern about Vanessa's mental health, while Whindersson Nunes stated that he had faced similar crises, sympathizing with her situation, classifying the episode as a situation of mania.[34][35][36]
On January 19, Vanessa left the program.[37] In an interview with Fantástico, the influencer revealed that she had an acute psychotic condition.[38][39]
Vanessa was also invited to participate in the program Altas Horas to discuss her mental health and shared the following statement:
I am fine. Now I'm in treatment, but I'm still scared. Admitting that you are sick is a little scary, but it is part of the process, the treatment and also to talk a little about mental health. I'm happy to talk to you about this here. I'm fine, but I want to get even better.
— said the digital influencer to Serginho Groisman.[40]

In the past year alone, she’s been spotted with KATSEYE, Meghan Trainor, and Tate McRae. Nevertheless, she still gets the same onslaught of comments with each video drop: “How do I be you? You’re so lucky!”
To chalk it all up to luck, however, would be a disservice to the 19-year-old dancing queen. Guerrero is currently the Philippines’ most-followed TikTok creator with over 45 million followers (and around a billion likes). Her virality extends to YouTube, where an audience of almost 16 million subscribers has watched her grow up.
The most chronically online among us might recognize Guerrero as the baby girl bopping along to “Despacito,” while her older brother Ranz Kyle drove her to an undisclosed location. Running a little past a minute long, it soon spawned a dance craze in the same vein as the Harlem Shake and landed the sibling duo a slot in the 2017 YouTube Rewind, an annual video series featuring the hottest trendmakers of the past year.
Born to a family that valued and nurtured talents in the arts, Guerrero was a shy kid in Manila who turned to movement as a means of self-expression. Her earliest home videos show her trying to imitate Michael Jackson’s distinct dance routines. Behind the camera was her brother, who already had a past life as a member of the Filipino boy band Chicser. (Guerrero’s debut video appearance was actually in their 2011 cover of “Teach Me How to Dougie.”)
Kyle found something special and funny in his little sister’s innate talent, and he began featuring her in his videos as he made the jump to vlogging. Post-”Despacito,” Guerrero’s parents decided to homeschool her. “Initially, I really didn’t think about the views, followers, likes, or anything. I wanted to share my love for dance and show our family spending time together,” Guerrero says.
The pandemic marked yet another turning point in Guerrero’s burgeoning career: like the rest of us, she was grooving to “Say So” and “Supalonely,” but in a more capable fashion. Her feel-good trendsetting content soon introduced her to a new audience in search of light in dark times. Guerrero says that many of her most-replicated dance challenges, like “Booty Wurk,” and “Give It Up,” come from just surrendering to a beat that takes over her body. “Surprisingly, my dance trends that go viral are the ones that just come out of nowhere: I’d be playing the song in my room and then all of a sudden, a choreography would come to mind,” she says. “I’d upload it and then be totally shocked the next day that so many people decided to try it too.
Similarly, the vlogs she posts to her channel of 15 million subscribers don’t follow any specific formula. She gravitates towards content of her parents and siblings bonding together, which resonates with her family-centric Filipino audience — even as they’re ignoring their baby sister Natalia or turning Ranz’s room into a ball pit as a prank.
It was only a matter of time before this effortless authenticity attracted some of her favorite artists. While some collaborations are business deals with terms that are negotiated from the start, many of these interactions started with them sliding directly into Guerrero’s DMs and building a foundation of friendship. It’s safe to say, though, that no moment beats getting noticed by her long-time celebrity crush.
“When Jungkook followed me, I started jumping in my room because I couldn’t believe that it was true,” she says with infectious enthusiasm about BTS’s youngest member. “I even messaged him and said, ‘Oh my god, is this true?’ and when he replied with ‘Yes!’, I freaked out again.”
Last February, yet another BTS member took notice of Guerrero: J-hope both followed and shot her a message, asking if she could teach him how to use TikTok. (The two mutuals even met up during his recently concluded Hope On The Stage Manila leg.) “I was literally in the car on the way to an event when I saw it through a tweet, and I had to check if it was real multiple times because I couldn’t believe it at all,” she says. “BTS is the best K-pop group ever to me.”
Among her other admirers and past collaborators include NCT Dream, Sabrina Carpenter, and even Chef Gordon Ramsay, whom she was “honestly terrified” of back in childhood. (“He’s way nicer than we all think,” she says.) I ask her lightheartedly if she’s going to take this as her first foray into food, which makes her break into a laugh. Probably not, but she’s very willing to explore other fields.
As avid viewers of her livestreams would know, Guerrero has always dabbled in music. It was once an annual tradition for her to collaborate with Ranz on songs centered around the same message of positivity and empowerment. But now, she’s eager to discover what other genres she could pursue.
Current collaborations with Louis Vuitton and BYS Cosmetics also point to her growing influence in the world of fashion and beauty: “I’m trying to be more intentional with the way I present myself, so I’m experimenting a lot right now,” she says. “I’m taking a lot of inspiration from what I see on Pinterest and TikTok and trying to inject my own flavor based on what I’m comfortable with.” We get a sense of her eclectic sensibilities on her Instagram: one day, she’s Cupid in a crimson bodysuit with an accent belt, only for her to dress down into her signature statement tee and sneakers the next.
Unlike her approach to dance, Guerrero’s outlook towards life is less based on vibes. “I think it’s important to go with the flow but I do appreciate structure. I’ll let things happen in a natural way but when it comes to choosing which people to keep in my immediate circle, carving out a space I can be comfortable in, making my own schedule, and having a say in my recent projects, I want to be more conscious now.”
Influencers may find it hard to strike a balance between the personal and public-facing, especially when every moment can be monetized. But Guerrero has never felt the need to follow any trends, or cave to the demands of the majority. “I think it’s easy to get caught up in what people expect of me, but in the end, I always do what feels right for me,” she says. “I want to stay true to who I am.”
Even though her career is pretty much in full force, Guerrero has no plans of letting her personal goals take the backseat. Some of the items on her bucket list for the year? Going to Coachella; exploring Paris; and meeting the likes of Tyla and Jungkook.
Of course, as someone who grew up in the public eye, she also strives to attain simple joys, such as traveling with her close group of friends. “I never got to have sleepovers growing up, so when my friends and I went to Japan and stayed in the same Airbnb, it was the closest I had ever gotten to that experience,” she says. “I loved shopping the whole day and getting home and doing little hauls with them. It was so memorable for me.”
I ask her if there’s anything jarring about having the entire archive of her life available online for public viewing, but she’s never seen it that way.
“I’m grateful that people have seen different versions of me over the years,” Niana Guerrero says. “And though my interests and style and mindset will evolve, I’ll grow and document as I go.”

Vanessa Lopes Ramalho[1] (born July 5, 2001)[2] is a Brazilian digital influencer and dancer, known for having more than 30.5 million followers on TikTok, where she is successful with her choreographies.[3][4] In 2024, she was a participant in the twenty-fourth edition of the reality show Big Brother Brasil; Vanessa's participation was brief and generated controversy.[5][6]
Biography
[edit]Lopes was born in Brasília, but moved to Recife as a child. She created a TikTok account while she was at university and, during the COVID-19 pandemic, started recording and posting dance videos on the app. As of January 2024, Lopes has 30.2 million followers on TikTok and 14.3 million followers on Instagram. She presents the podcast Não é TPM with Fernanda Schneider, Gabriela Mag, Victória Collen, Isa Paoli and Vivi Wanderley.[7][8]
In 2024, Vanessa Lopes was a member of the "Celebrity" group in the 24th season of Big Brother Brasil. In January of the same year, her TikTok account had a total of 1 billion likes.[9][10]
Personal life
[edit]Relationships and personal interests
[edit]Vanessa Lopes is openly bisexual.[11][12] In June 2021, she began dating football player and TikToker Ricardo Rêgo, which lasted six months. Vanessa also had involvement with actor João Guilherme,[13] and publicly shared interactions with other personalities, such as Luísa Sonza,[14] Lara Silva, Gabi Lopes and Gabriel Medina.[15][16]
On social media, Lopes also highlights her passion for sports, being a Flamengo[17][18] fan and a footvolley player,[19] as well as demonstrating an interest in surfing, an activity she also does during her free time.[20]
Accident
[edit]After completing high school, Lopes had the desire to go on exchange and study abroad. However, during a trip with a friend, DJ Alan Maciel, she was hit by a driver who fled the scene, near Porto de Galinhas. They were on their way to a show when their vehicle had a flat tire. At the time of the exchange, a car hit them and threw them about 20 meters away. Vanessa was holding the flashlight so that Maciel could have a better view when changing the tire.[21] At the time of the accident, Vanessa was just 18 years old, and this traumatic experience made her rethink the idea of living far from family and friends, leading her to conclude that it wasn't worth going abroad.[22]
A year after the road tragedy, Lopes decided to split her time between attending college for marketing and getting involved in creating digital content.[23]
Mental health
[edit]Throughout her participation in BBB 24, Lopes revealed that she was confronting emotional triggers from past traumas, showing signs of psychological instability. Her instability increased when comments appeared alleging that she was a superficial person, constantly looking in the mirror, and that her attitudes, including her moments of crying, were not genuine.[24] When faced with the accusations, Vanessa remembered difficult situations she had faced before the reality show, clarifying that her habit of looking in the mirror was a strategy to deal with the temporomandibular disorder she faces and that she seeks to recover.[25] In the following days, her emotional instability intensified, reflected in her increasingly weakened participation. Vanessa also revealed that she felt persecuted, even thinking that she was being persecuted and affected on purpose.[26][27] Furthermore, she made frequent references to George Orwell's book 1984, which inspired the creation of Big Brother.[28] In a peculiar moment, she questioned whether her confinement colleagues were actors, highlighting the depth of her psychological discomfort during the program.[29] Vanessa also got involved in intriguing situations with other participants and even threw away all her colleagues' toothbrushes while cleaning the bathroom.[30][31]
Vanessa's behaviors raised concerns among viewers, who expressed fears about her mental health, urging the show's production team to intervene.[32] There was also speculation about the possibility of a psychotic break during the events.[33] On social media, personalities such as Bruna Marquezine, Jojo Todynho, Mel Maia and Deborah Secco also expressed concern about Vanessa's mental health, while Whindersson Nunes stated that he had faced similar crises, sympathizing with her situation, classifying the episode as a situation of mania.[34][35][36]
On January 19, Vanessa left the program.[37] In an interview with Fantástico, the influencer revealed that she had an acute psychotic condition.[38][39]
Vanessa was also invited to participate in the program Altas Horas to discuss her mental health and shared the following statement:
I am fine. Now I'm in treatment, but I'm still scared. Admitting that you are sick is a little scary, but it is part of the process, the treatment and also to talk a little about mental health. I'm happy to talk to you about this here. I'm fine, but I want to get even better.
— said the digital influencer to Serginho Groisman.[40]

**Charli D'Amelio: The Queen of TikTok**

Charli D'Amelio, the youngest sensation on TikTok, has captured the hearts of millions with her infectious dance moves and viral challenges. Born on March 14, 2002, in Miami, Florida, D'Amelio has quickly risen to stardom, becoming one of the most popular TikTok dancers in the world.

**A Step into Pop Culture**

D'Amelio's journey from the Miami suburb of Opa-Locka to the global stage is a testament to her talent and marketing prowess. With a career that spans beyond TikTok, she has ventured into music, fashion, and even acting, solidifying her place in the entertainment industry. Her breakout hit, "Peaches," in 2021, showcased her versatility and became one of the most streamed songs on the platform.

**The Art of Dance**

Charli D'Amelio's dance moves are not just a form of entertainment; they are a form of self-expression. Her ability to captivate audiences with her fluid movements and catchy choreography has made her a role model for young dancers everywhere. **The Power of Virality**

D'Amelio's viral success is a result of her strategic approach to content creation and marketing. She has a knack for identifying trends and leveraging them to her advantage. From her early days of uploading simple dance challenges to her more recent forays into music and fashion, D'Amelio has consistently evolved her persona and style to keep up with the ever-changing landscape of social media.

**Beyond TikTok**

While D'Amelio's career on TikTok is undoubtedly the most prominent, she has not shied away from exploring other platforms. Her collaborations with brands and her involvement in various social media initiatives demonstrate her adaptability and commitment to staying relevant in the digital age. D'Amelio's influence extends beyond TikTok, making her a significant figure in the world of social media and entertainment.

Charli D'Amelio is more than just a TikTok sensation; she is a cultural icon who has left an indelible mark on the digital age. With her unique style, strategic marketing, and boundless creativity, D'Amelio continues to inspire and entertain millions

(The two mutuals even met up during his recently concluded Hope On The Stage Manila leg.) “I was literally in the car on the way to an event when I saw it through a tweet, and I had to check if it was real multiple times because I couldn’t believe it at all,” she says. “BTS is the best K-pop group ever to me.”
Among her other admirers and past collaborators include NCT Dream, Sabrina Carpenter, and even Chef Gordon Ramsay, whom she was “honestly terrified” of back in childhood. (“He’s way nicer than we all think,” she says.) I ask her lightheartedly if she’s going to take this as her first foray into food, which makes her break into a laugh. Probably not, but she’s very willing to explore other fields.
As avid viewers of her livestreams would know, Guerrero has always dabbled in music. It was once an annual tradition for her to collaborate with Ranz on songs centered around the same message of positivity and empowerment. But now, she’s eager to discover what other genres she could pursue.
Current collaborations with Louis Vuitton and BYS Cosmetics also point to her growing influence in the world of fashion and beauty: “I’m trying to be more intentional with the way I present myself, so I’m experimenting a lot right now,” she says. “I’m taking a lot of inspiration from what I see on Pinterest and TikTok and trying to inject my own flavor based on what I’m comfortable with.” We get a sense of her eclectic sensibilities on her Instagram: one day, she’s Cupid in a crimson bodysuit with an accent belt, only for her to dress down into her signature statement tee and sneakers the next.
Unlike her approach to dance, Guerrero’s outlook towards life is less based on vibes. “I think it’s important to go with the flow but I do appreciate structure. I’ll let things happen in a natural way but when it comes to choosing which people to keep in my immediate circle, carving out a space I can be comfortable in, making my own schedule, and having a say in my recent projects, I want to be more conscious now.”
Influencers may find it hard to strike a balance between the personal and public-facing, especially when every moment can be monetized. But Guerrero has never felt the need to follow any trends, or cave to the demands of the majority. “I think it’s easy to get caught up in what people expect of me, but in the end, I always do what feels right for me,” she says. “I want to stay true to who I am.”
Even though her career is pretty much in full force, Guerrero has no plans of letting her personal goals take the backseat. Some of the items on her bucket list for the year? Going to Coachella; exploring Paris; and meeting the likes of Tyla and Jungkook.
Of course, as someone who grew up in the public eye, she also strives to attain simple joys, such as traveling with her close group of friends. “I never got to have sleepovers growing up, so when my friends and I went to Japan and stayed in the same Airbnb, it was the closest I had ever gotten to that experience,” she says. “I loved shopping the whole day and getting home and doing little hauls with them. It was so memorable for me.”
I ask her if there’s anything jarring about having the entire archive of her life available online for public viewing, but she’s never seen it that way.
“I’m grateful that people have seen different versions of me over the years,” Niana Guerrero says. “And though my interests and style and mindset will evolve, I’ll grow and document as I go.”

Vanessa Lopes Ramalho[1] (born July 5, 2001)[2] is a Brazilian digital influencer and dancer, known for having more than 30.5 million followers on TikTok, where she is successful with her choreographies.[3][4] In 2024, she was a participant in the twenty-fourth edition of the reality show Big Brother Brasil; Vanessa's participation was brief and generated controversy.[5][6]
Biography
[edit]Lopes was born in Brasília, but moved to Recife as a child. She created a TikTok account while she was at university and, during the COVID-19 pandemic, started recording and posting dance videos on the app. As of January 2024, Lopes has 30.2 million followers on TikTok and 14.3 million followers on Instagram. She presents the podcast Não é TPM with Fernanda Schneider, Gabriela Mag, Victória Collen, Isa Paoli and Vivi Wanderley.[7][8]
In 2024, Vanessa Lopes was a member of the "Celebrity" group in the 24th season of Big Brother Brasil. In January of the same year, her TikTok account had a total of 1 billion likes.[9][10]
Personal life
[edit]Relationships and personal interests
[edit]Vanessa Lopes is openly bisexual.[11][12] In June 2021, she began dating football player and TikToker Ricardo Rêgo, which lasted six months. Vanessa also had involvement with actor João Guilherme,[13] and publicly shared interactions with other personalities, such as Luísa Sonza,[14] Lara Silva, Gabi Lopes and Gabriel Medina.[15][16]
On social media, Lopes also highlights her passion for sports, being a Flamengo[17][18] fan and a footvolley player,[19] as well as demonstrating an interest in surfing, an activity she also does during her free time.[20]
Accident
[edit]After completing high school, Lopes had the desire to go on exchange and study abroad. However, during a trip with a friend, DJ Alan Maciel, she was hit by a driver who fled the scene, near Porto de Galinhas. They were on their way to a show when their vehicle had a flat tire. At the time of the exchange, a car hit them and threw them about 20 meters away. Vanessa was holding the flashlight so that Maciel could have a better view when changing the tire.[21] At the time of the accident, Vanessa was just 18 years old, and this traumatic experience made her rethink the idea of living far from family and friends, leading her to conclude that it wasn't worth going abroad.[22]
A year after the road tragedy, Lopes decided to split her time between attending college for marketing and getting involved in creating digital content.[23]
Mental health
[edit]Throughout her participation in BBB 24, Lopes revealed that she was confronting emotional triggers from past traumas, showing signs of psychological instability. Her instability increased when comments appeared alleging that she was a superficial person, constantly looking in the mirror, and that her attitudes, including her moments of crying, were not genuine.[24] When faced with the accusations, Vanessa remembered difficult situations she had faced before the reality show, clarifying that her habit of looking in the mirror was a strategy to deal with the temporomandibular disorder she faces and that she seeks to recover.[25] In the following days, her emotional instability intensified, reflected in her increasingly weakened participation. Vanessa also revealed that she felt persecuted, even thinking that she was being persecuted and affected on purpose.[26][27] Furthermore, she made frequent references to George Orwell's book 1984, which inspired the creation of Big Brother.[28] In a peculiar moment, she questioned whether her confinement colleagues were actors, highlighting the depth of her psychological discomfort during the program.[29] Vanessa also got involved in intriguing situations with other participants and even threw away all her colleagues' toothbrushes while cleaning the bathroom.[30][31]
Vanessa's behaviors raised concerns among viewers, who expressed fears about her mental health, urging the show's production team to intervene.[32] There was also speculation about the possibility of a psychotic break during the events.[33] On social media, personalities such as Bruna Marquezine, Jojo Todynho, Mel Maia and Deborah Secco also expressed concern about Vanessa's mental health, while Whindersson Nunes stated that he had faced similar crises, sympathizing with her situation, classifying the episode as a situation of mania.[34][35][36]
On January 19, Vanessa left the program.[37] In an interview with Fantástico, the influencer revealed that she had an acute psychotic condition.[38][39]
Vanessa was also invited to participate in the program Altas Horas to discuss her mental health and shared the following statement:
I am fine. Now I'm in treatment, but I'm still scared. Admitting that you are sick is a little scary, but it is part of the process, the treatment and also to talk a little about mental health. I'm happy to talk to you about this here. I'm fine, but I want to get even better.
— said the digital influencer to Serginho Groisman.[40]

### Charli D'Amelio: The New Face of TikTok's Creators

In a world where every second is consumed by the endless stream of videos, Charli D'Amelio stands out like a beacon of creativity and digital influence. The 21-year-old TikTok sensation has become a household name, making her way into the coveted ranks of Time's "Titans" of 2025 creators list. This groundbreaking recognition not only highlights her talent but also underscores the growing influence of young, social media influencers in today's digital landscape.

#### Charli D'Amelio: The TikTok Phenomenon

Charli D'Amelio, born on September 17, 2000, in Palm Desert, California, has been a force in the world of social media for the past decade. Her journey from a shy teenager to a global sensation began when she uploaded her first video to the platform in 2017. The video, titled "I'm a shy girl, but I'm not a scared girl," quickly gained traction, and her unique style and approach to content creation quickly made her stand out.

D'Amelio's videos are known for their upbeat, energetic vibe, often featuring her quirky sense of humor and her love for animals. Her TikTok account, @Charli, has amassed over 200 million followers, making her one of the most followed creators on the platform. Her success has not only transformed her into a global brand but has also paved the way for other young influencers to follow in her footsteps.

#### The Rise of Charli D'Amelio: From Shy Teen to Global Star

D'Amelio's rise to fame is a testament to her ability to connect with her audience on a personal level. Her videos are a mix of humor, self-expression, and genuine moments, which resonates with many viewers. She has also mastered the art of storytelling, using her platform to share personal experiences and insights, which have helped her build a loyal following.

One of the key factors behind D'Amelio's success is her authenticity. She has been open about her struggles with anxiety and her journey to overcome it, which has resonated with many viewers. This authenticity has allowed her to form a deep connection with her audience, creating a sense of relatability that has been crucial in her rise to fame.

#### The Impact of Charli D'Amelio on the Social Media Landscape

Not everyone gets to say that they danced alongside BLACKPINK’s Lisa. But then again, online sensation Niana Guerrero isn’t just anybody.
In a short TikTok from March, the two perform “FVCK UP THE WORLD” with the synchronicity and familiarity of long-time teammates. “But I remember telling her before we started that I was so nervous, and she had told me that she was nervous too. Imagine that!” Guerrero tells Teen Vogue over Zoom. It’s not her first celebrity collaboration — far from it, actually. In the past year alone, she’s been spotted with KATSEYE, Meghan Trainor, and Tate McRae. Nevertheless, she still gets the same onslaught of comments with each video drop: “How do I be you? You’re so lucky!”
To chalk it all up to luck, however, would be a disservice to the 19-year-old dancing queen. Guerrero is currently the Philippines’ most-followed TikTok creator with over 45 million followers (and around a billion likes). Her virality extends to YouTube, where an audience of almost 16 million subscribers has watched her grow up.
The most chronically online among us might recognize Guerrero as the baby girl bopping along to “Despacito,” while her older brother Ranz Kyle drove her to an undisclosed location. Running a little past a minute long, it soon spawned a dance craze in the same vein as the Harlem Shake and landed the sibling duo a slot in the 2017 YouTube Rewind, an annual video series featuring the hottest trendmakers of the past year.
Born to a family that valued and nurtured talents in the arts, Guerrero was a shy kid in Manila who turned to movement as a means of self-expression. Her earliest home videos show her trying to imitate Michael Jackson’s distinct dance routines. Behind the camera was her brother, who already had a past life as a member of the Filipino boy band Chicser. (Guerrero’s debut video appearance was actually in their 2011 cover of “Teach Me How to Dougie.”)
Kyle found something special and funny in his little sister’s innate talent, and he began featuring her in his videos as he made the jump to vlogging. Post-”Despacito,” Guerrero’s parents decided to homeschool her. “Initially, I really didn’t think about the views, followers, likes, or anything. I wanted to share my love for dance and show our family spending time together,” Guerrero says.
The pandemic marked yet another turning point in Guerrero’s burgeoning career: like the rest of us, she was grooving to “Say So” and “Supalonely,” but in a more capable fashion. Her feel-good trendsetting content soon introduced her to a new audience in search of light in dark times. Guerrero says that many of her most-replicated dance challenges, like “Booty Wurk,” and “Give It Up,” come from just surrendering to a beat that takes over her body. “Surprisingly, my dance trends that go viral are the ones that just come out of nowhere: I’d be playing the song in my room and then all of a sudden, a choreography would come to mind,” she says. “I’d upload it and then be totally shocked the next day that so many people decided to try it too.
Similarly, the vlogs she posts to her channel of 15 million subscribers don’t follow any specific formula. She gravitates towards content of her parents and siblings bonding together, which resonates with her family-centric Filipino audience — even as they’re ignoring their baby sister Natalia or turning Ranz’s room into a ball pit as a prank.
It was only a matter of time before this effortless authenticity attracted some of her favorite artists. While some collaborations are business deals with terms that are negotiated from the start, many of these interactions started with them sliding directly into Guerrero’s DMs and building a foundation of friendship. It’s safe to say, though, that no moment beats getting noticed by her long-time celebrity crush.
“When Jungkook followed me, I started jumping in my room because I couldn’t believe that it was true,” she says with infectious enthusiasm about BTS’s youngest member. “I even messaged him and said, ‘Oh my god, is this true?’ and when he replied with ‘Yes!’, I freaked out again.”
Last February, yet another BTS member took notice of Guerrero: J-hope both followed and shot her a message, asking if she could teach him how to use TikTok. (The two mutuals even met up during his recently concluded Hope On The Stage Manila leg.) “I was literally in the car on the way to an event when I saw it through a tweet, and I had to check if it was real multiple times because I couldn’t believe it at all,” she says. “BTS is the best K-pop group ever to me.”
Among her other admirers and past collaborators include NCT Dream, Sabrina Carpenter, and even Chef Gordon Ramsay, whom she was “honestly terrified” of back in childhood. (“He’s way nicer than we all think,” she says.) I ask her lightheartedly if she’s going to take this as her first foray into food, which makes her break into a laugh. Probably not, but she’s very willing to explore other fields.
As avid viewers of her livestreams would know, Guerrero has always dabbled in music. It was once an annual tradition for her to collaborate with Ranz on songs centered around the same message of positivity and empowerment. But now, she’s eager to discover what other genres she could pursue.
Current collaborations with Louis Vuitton and BYS Cosmetics also point to her growing influence in the world of fashion and beauty: “I’m trying to be more intentional with the way I present myself, so I’m experimenting a lot right now,” she says. “I’m taking a lot of inspiration from what I see on Pinterest and TikTok and trying to inject my own flavor based on what I’m comfortable with.” We get a sense of her eclectic sensibilities on her Instagram: one day, she’s Cupid in a crimson bodysuit with an accent belt, only for her to dress down into her signature statement tee and sneakers the next.
Unlike her approach to dance, Guerrero’s outlook towards life is less based on vibes. “I think it’s important to go with the flow but I do appreciate structure. I’ll let things happen in a natural way but when it comes to choosing which people to keep in my immediate circle, carving out a space I can be comfortable in, making my own schedule, and having a say in my recent projects, I want to be more conscious now.”
Influencers may find it hard to strike a balance between the personal and public-facing, especially when every moment can be monetized. But Guerrero has never felt the need to follow any trends, or cave to the demands of the majority. “I think it’s easy to get caught up in what people expect of me, but in the end, I always do what feels right for me,” she says. “I want to stay true to who I am.”
Even though her career is pretty much in full force, Guerrero has no plans of letting her personal goals take the backseat. Some of the items on her bucket list for the year? Going to Coachella; exploring Paris; and meeting the likes of Tyla and Jungkook.
Of course, as someone who grew up in the public eye, she also strives to attain simple joys, such as traveling with her close group of friends. “I never got to have sleepovers growing up, so when my friends and I went to Japan and stayed in the same Airbnb, it was the closest I had ever gotten to that experience,” she says. “I loved shopping the whole day and getting home and doing little hauls with them. It was so memorable for me.”
I ask her if there’s anything jarring about having the entire archive of her life available online for public viewing, but she’s never seen it that way.
“I’m grateful that people have seen different versions of me over the years,” Niana Guerrero says. “And though my interests and style and mindset will evolve, I’ll grow and document as I go.”

Vanessa Lopes Ramalho[1] (born July 5, 2001)[2] is a Brazilian digital influencer and dancer, known for having more than 30.5 million followers on TikTok, where she is successful with her choreographies.[3][4] In 2024, she was a participant in the twenty-fourth edition of the reality show Big Brother Brasil; Vanessa's participation was brief and generated controversy.[5][6]
Biography
[edit]Lopes was born in Brasília, but moved to Recife as a child. She created a TikTok account while she was at university and, during the COVID-19 pandemic, started recording and posting dance videos on the app. As of January 2024, Lopes has 30.2 million followers on TikTok and 14.3 million followers on Instagram. She presents the podcast Não é TPM with Fernanda Schneider, Gabriela Mag, Victória Collen, Isa Paoli and Vivi Wanderley.[7][8]
In 2024, Vanessa Lopes was a member of the "Celebrity" group in the 24th season of Big Brother Brasil. In January of the same year, her TikTok account had a total of 1 billion likes.[9][10]
Personal life
[edit]Relationships and personal interests
[edit]Vanessa Lopes is openly bisexual.[11][12] In June 2021, she began dating football player and TikToker Ricardo Rêgo, which lasted six months. Vanessa also had involvement with actor João Guilherme,[13] and publicly shared interactions with other personalities, such as Luísa Sonza,[14] Lara Silva, Gabi Lopes and Gabriel Medina.[15][16]
On social media, Lopes also highlights her passion for sports, being a Flamengo[17][18] fan and a footvolley player,[19] as well as demonstrating an interest in surfing, an activity she also does during her free time.[20]
Accident
[edit]After completing high school, Lopes had the desire to go on exchange and study abroad. However, during a trip with a friend, DJ Alan Maciel, she was hit by a driver who fled the scene, near Porto de Galinhas. They were on their way to a show when their vehicle had a flat tire. At the time of the exchange, a car hit them and threw them about 20 meters away. Vanessa was holding the flashlight so that Maciel could have a better view when changing the tire.[21] At the time of the accident, Vanessa was just 18 years old, and this traumatic experience made her rethink the idea of living far from family and friends, leading her to conclude that it wasn't worth going abroad.[22]
A year after the road tragedy, Lopes decided to split her time between attending college for marketing and getting involved in creating digital content.[23]
Mental health
[edit]Throughout her participation in BBB 24, Lopes revealed that she was confronting emotional triggers from past traumas, showing signs of psychological instability. Her instability increased when comments appeared alleging that she was a superficial person, constantly looking in the mirror, and that her attitudes, including her moments of crying, were not genuine.[24] When faced with the accusations, Vanessa remembered difficult situations she had faced before the reality show, clarifying that her habit of looking in the mirror was a strategy to deal with the temporomandibular disorder she faces and that she seeks to recover.[25] In the following days, her emotional instability intensified, reflected in her increasingly weakened participation. Vanessa also revealed that she felt persecuted, even thinking that she was being persecuted and affected on purpose.[26][27] Furthermore, she made frequent references to George Orwell's book 1984, which inspired the creation of Big Brother.[28] In a peculiar moment, she questioned whether her confinement colleagues were actors, highlighting the depth of her psychological discomfort during the program.[29] Vanessa also got involved in intriguing situations with other participants and even threw away all her colleagues' toothbrushes while cleaning the bathroom.[30][31]
Vanessa's behaviors raised concerns among viewers, who expressed fears about her mental health, urging the show's production team to intervene.[32] There was also speculation about the possibility of a psychotic break during the events.[33] On social media, personalities such as Bruna Marquezine, Jojo Todynho, Mel Maia and Deborah Secco also expressed concern about Vanessa's mental health, while Whindersson Nunes stated that he had faced similar crises, sympathizing with her situation, classifying the episode as a situation of mania.[34][35][36]
On January 19, Vanessa left the program.[37] In an interview with Fantástico, the influencer revealed that she had an acute psychotic condition.[38][39]
Vanessa was also invited to participate in the program Altas Horas to discuss her mental health and shared the following statement:
I am fine. Now I'm in treatment, but I'm still scared. Admitting that you are sick is a little scary, but it is part of the process, the treatment and also to talk a little about mental health. I'm happy to talk to you about this here. I'm fine, but I want to get even better.
— said the digital influencer to Serginho Groisman.[40]

In the ever-evolving landscape of social media, few names command as much attention as Charli D'Amelio. Known for her electrifying dance moves and viral TikTok hits, D'Amelio has established herself as the undisputed queen of the dance world. With over 111 million followers on TikTok, she is the most popular TikTok dancer based on the information provided.

D'Amelio's journey to stardom began with her TikTok challenge "No Limits," which quickly went viral, capturing the hearts of millions. The song "I Don't Care" by Cardi B and Megan Thee Stallion, which was featured in the video, further propelled her to fame. Her energetic dance moves and catchy tunes have become synonymous with the TikTok experience, making her a household name.

Beyond her viral hits, D'Amelio has also ventured into other areas of entertainment. In 2020, she made her debut on the big screen with the action-packed film "Panda," where she played the role of a young girl in a Chinese village. Her performance was praised for its authenticity and the film's success helped solidify her status as a rising star in the entertainment industry.

D'Amelio's influence extends far beyond her music and dance. She has also been a vocal advocate for mental health and has used her platform to promote positivity and self-love. Her "Charli's Kindness" challenge encourages viewers to spread kindness and positivity, further cementing her reputation as a role model for young people.

As TikTok continues to grow and evolve, Charli D'Amelio's impact on the platform is undeniable. Her dedication to dance, her talent for viral content, and her commitment to positivity have made her one of the most popular and influential dancers on the platform. With her continued success on TikTok and beyond, D'Amelio is poised to become a household name in the entertainment world.

Not everyone gets to say that they danced alongside BLACKPINK’s Lisa. But then again, online sensation Niana Guerrero isn’t just anybody.
In a short TikTok from March, the two perform “FVCK UP THE WORLD” with the synchronicity and familiarity of long-time teammates. “But I remember telling her before we started that I was so nervous, and she had told me that she was nervous too. Imagine that!” Guerrero tells Teen Vogue over Zoom. It’s not her first celebrity collaboration — far from it, actually. In the past year alone, she’s been spotted with KATSEYE, Meghan Trainor, and Tate McRae. Nevertheless, she still gets the same onslaught of comments with each video drop: “How do I be you? You’re so lucky!”
To chalk it all up to luck, however, would be a disservice to the 19-year-old dancing queen. Guerrero is currently the Philippines’ most-followed TikTok creator with over 45 million followers (and around a billion likes). Her virality extends to YouTube, where an audience of almost 16 million subscribers has watched her grow up.
The most chronically online among us might recognize Guerrero as the baby girl bopping along to “Despacito,” while her older brother Ranz Kyle drove her to an undisclosed location. Running a little past a minute long, it soon spawned a dance craze in the same vein as the Harlem Shake and landed the sibling duo a slot in the 2017 YouTube Rewind, an annual video series featuring the hottest trendmakers of the past year.
Born to a family that valued and nurtured talents in the arts, Guerrero was a shy kid in Manila who turned to movement as a means of self-expression. Her earliest home videos show her trying to imitate Michael Jackson’s distinct dance routines. Behind the camera was her brother, who already had a past life as a member of the Filipino boy band Chicser. (Guerrero’s debut video appearance was actually in their 2011 cover of “Teach Me How to Dougie.”)
Kyle found something special and funny in his little sister’s innate talent, and he began featuring her in his videos as he made the jump to vlogging. Post-”Despacito,” Guerrero’s parents decided to homeschool her. “Initially, I really didn’t think about the views, followers, likes, or anything. I wanted to share my love for dance and show our family spending time together,” Guerrero says.
The pandemic marked yet another turning point in Guerrero’s burgeoning career: like the rest of us, she was grooving to “Say So” and “Supalonely,” but in a more capable fashion. Her feel-good trendsetting content soon introduced her to a new audience in search of light in dark times. Guerrero says that many of her most-replicated dance challenges, like “Booty Wurk,” and “Give It Up,” come from just surrendering to a beat that takes over her body. “Surprisingly, my dance trends that go viral are the ones that just come out of nowhere: I’d be playing the song in my room and then all of a sudden, a choreography would come to mind,” she says. “I’d upload it and then be totally shocked the next day that so many people decided to try it too.
Similarly, the vlogs she posts to her channel of 15 million subscribers don’t follow any specific formula. She gravitates towards content of her parents and siblings bonding together, which resonates with her family-centric Filipino audience — even as they’re ignoring their baby sister Natalia or turning Ranz’s room into a ball pit as a prank.
It was only a matter of time before this effortless authenticity attracted some of her favorite artists. While some collaborations are business deals with terms that are negotiated from the start, many of these interactions started with them sliding directly into Guerrero’s DMs and building a foundation of friendship. It’s safe to say, though, that no moment beats getting noticed by her long-time celebrity crush.
“When Jungkook followed me, I started jumping in my room because I couldn’t believe that it was true,” she says with infectious enthusiasm about BTS’s youngest member. “I even messaged him and said, ‘Oh my god, is this true?’ and when he replied with ‘Yes!’, I freaked out again.”
Last February, yet another BTS member took notice of Guerrero: J-hope both followed and shot her a message, asking if she could teach him how to use TikTok. (The two mutuals even met up during his recently concluded Hope On The Stage Manila leg.) “I was literally in the car on the way to an event when I saw it through a tweet, and I had to check if it was real multiple times because I couldn’t believe it at all,” she says. “BTS is the best K-pop group ever to me.”
Among her other admirers and past collaborators include NCT Dream, Sabrina Carpenter, and even Chef Gordon Ramsay, whom she was “honestly terrified” of back in childhood. (“He’s way nicer than we all think,” she says.) I ask her lightheartedly if she’s going to take this as her first foray into food, which makes her break into a laugh. Probably not, but she’s very willing to explore other fields.
As avid viewers of her livestreams would know, Guerrero has always dabbled in music. It was once an annual tradition for her to collaborate with Ranz on songs centered around the same message of positivity and empowerment. But now, she’s eager to discover what other genres she could pursue.
Current collaborations with Louis Vuitton and BYS Cosmetics also point to her growing influence in the world of fashion and beauty: “I’m trying to be more intentional with the way I present myself, so I’m experimenting a lot right now,” she says. “I’m taking a lot of inspiration from what I see on Pinterest and TikTok and trying to inject my own flavor based on what I’m comfortable with.” We get a sense of her eclectic sensibilities on her Instagram: one day, she’s Cupid in a crimson bodysuit with an accent belt, only for her to dress down into her signature statement tee and sneakers the next.
Unlike her approach to dance, Guerrero’s outlook towards life is less based on vibes. “I think it’s important to go with the flow but I do appreciate structure. I’ll let things happen in a natural way but when it comes to choosing which people to keep in my immediate circle, carving out a space I can be comfortable in, making my own schedule, and having a say in my recent projects, I want to be more conscious now.”
Influencers may find it hard to strike a balance between the personal and public-facing, especially when every moment can be monetized. But Guerrero has never felt the need to follow any trends, or cave to the demands of the majority. “I think it’s easy to get caught up in what people expect of me, but in the end, I always do what feels right for me,” she says. “I want to stay true to who I am.”
Even though her career is pretty much in full force, Guerrero has no plans of letting her personal goals take the backseat. Some of the items on her bucket list for the year? Going to Coachella; exploring Paris; and meeting the likes of Tyla and Jungkook.
Of course, as someone who grew up in the public eye, she also strives to attain simple joys, such as traveling with her close group of friends. “I never got to have sleepovers growing up, so when my friends and I went to Japan and stayed in the same Airbnb, it was the closest I had ever gotten to that experience,” she says. “I loved shopping the whole day and getting home and doing little hauls with them. It was so memorable for me.”
I ask her if there’s anything jarring about having the entire archive of her life available online for public viewing, but she’s never seen it that way.
“I’m grateful that people have seen different versions of me over the years,” Niana Guerrero says. “And though my interests and style and mindset will evolve, I’ll grow and document as I go.”

Vanessa's behaviors raised concerns among viewers, who expressed fears about her mental health, urging the show's production team to intervene.[32] There was also speculation about the possibility of a psychotic break during the events.[33] On social media, personalities such as Bruna Marquezine, Jojo Todynho, Mel Maia and Deborah Secco also expressed concern about Vanessa's mental health, while Whindersson Nunes stated that he had faced similar crises, sympathizing with her situation, classifying the episode as a situation of mania.[34][35][36]
On January 19, Vanessa left the program.[37] In an interview with Fantástico, the influencer revealed that she had an acute psychotic condition.[38][39]
Vanessa was also invited to participate in the program Altas Horas to discuss her mental health and shared the following statement:
I am fine. Now I'm in treatment, but I'm still scared. Admitting that you are sick is a little scary, but it is part of the process, the treatment and also to talk a little about mental health. I'm happy to talk to you about this here. I'm fine, but I want to get even better.
— said the digital influencer to Serginho Groisman.[40]

Not everyone gets to say that they danced alongside BLACKPINK’s Lisa. But then again, online sensation Niana Guerrero isn’t just anybody.
In a short TikTok from March, the two perform “FVCK UP THE WORLD” with the synchronicity and familiarity of long-time teammates. “But I remember telling her before we started that I was so nervous, and she had told me that she was nervous too. Imagine that!” Guerrero tells Teen Vogue over Zoom. It’s not her first celebrity collaboration — far from it, actually. In the past year alone, she’s been spotted with KATSEYE, Meghan Trainor, and Tate McRae. Nevertheless, she still gets the same onslaught of comments with each video drop: “How do I be you? You’re so lucky!”
To chalk it all up to luck, however, would be a disservice to the 19-year-old dancing queen. Guerrero is currently the Philippines’ most-followed TikTok creator with over 45 million followers (and around a billion likes). Her virality extends to YouTube, where an audience of almost 16 million subscribers has watched her grow up.
The most chronically online among us might recognize Guerrero as the baby girl bopping along to “Despacito,” while her older brother Ranz Kyle drove her to an undisclosed location. Running a little past a minute long, it soon spawned a dance craze in the same vein as the Harlem Shake and landed the sibling duo a slot in the 2017 YouTube Rewind, an annual video series featuring the hottest trendmakers of the past year.
Born to a family that valued and nurtured talents in the arts, Guerrero was a shy kid in Manila who turned to movement as a means of self-expression. Her earliest home videos show her trying to imitate Michael Jackson’s distinct dance routines. Behind the camera was her brother, who already had a past life as a member of the Filipino boy band Chicser. (Guerrero’s debut video appearance was actually in their 2011 cover of “Teach Me How to Dougie.”)
Kyle found something special and funny in his little sister’s innate talent, and he began featuring her in his videos as he made the jump to vlogging. Post-”Despacito,” Guerrero’s parents decided to homeschool her. “Initially, I really didn’t think about the views, followers, likes, or anything. I wanted to share my love for dance and show our family spending time together,” Guerrero says.
The pandemic marked yet another turning point in Guerrero’s burgeoning career: like the rest of us, she was grooving to “Say So” and “Supalonely,” but in a more capable fashion. Her feel-good trendsetting content soon introduced her to a new audience in search of light in dark times. Guerrero says that many of her most-replicated dance challenges, like “Booty Wurk,” and “Give It Up,” come from just surrendering to a beat that takes over her body. “Surprisingly, my dance trends that go viral are the ones that just come out of nowhere: I’d be playing the song in my room and then all of a sudden, a choreography would come to mind,” she says. “I’d upload it and then be totally shocked the next day that so many people decided to try it too.
Similarly, the vlogs she posts to her channel of 15 million subscribers don’t follow any specific formula. She gravitates towards content of her parents and siblings bonding together, which resonates with her family-centric Filipino audience — even as they’re ignoring their baby sister Natalia or turning Ranz’s room into a ball pit as a prank.
It was only a matter of time before this effortless authenticity attracted some of her favorite artists. While some collaborations are business deals with terms that are negotiated from the start, many of these interactions started with them sliding directly into Guerrero’s DMs and building a foundation of friendship. It’s safe to say, though, that no moment beats getting noticed by her long-time celebrity crush.
“When Jungkook followed me, I started jumping in my room because I couldn’t believe that it was true,” she says with infectious enthusiasm about BTS’s youngest member. “I even messaged him and said, ‘Oh my god, is this true?’ and when he replied with ‘Yes!’, I freaked out again.”
Last February, yet another BTS member took notice of Guerrero: J-hope both followed and shot her a message, asking if she could teach him how to use TikTok. (The two mutuals even met up during his recently concluded Hope On The Stage Manila leg.) “I was literally in the car on the way to an event when I saw it through a tweet, and I had to check if it was real multiple times because I couldn’t believe it at all,” she says. “BTS is the best K-pop group ever to me.”
Among her other admirers and past collaborators include NCT Dream, Sabrina Carpenter, and even Chef Gordon Ramsay, whom she was “honestly terrified” of back in childhood. (“He’s way nicer than we all think,” she says.) I ask her lightheartedly if she’s going to take this as her first foray into food, which makes her break into a laugh. Probably not, but she’s very willing to explore other fields.
As avid viewers of her livestreams would know, Guerrero has always dabbled in music. It was once an annual tradition for her to collaborate with Ranz on songs centered around the same message of positivity and empowerment. But now, she’s eager to discover what other genres she could pursue.
Current collaborations with Louis Vuitton and BYS Cosmetics also point to her growing influence in the world of fashion and beauty: “I’m trying to be more intentional with the way I present myself, so I’m experimenting a lot right now,” she says. “I’m taking a lot of inspiration from what I see on Pinterest and TikTok and trying to inject my own flavor based on what I’m comfortable with.” We get a sense of her eclectic sensibilities on her Instagram: one day, she’s Cupid in a crimson bodysuit with an accent belt, only for her to dress down into her signature statement tee and sneakers the next.
Unlike her approach to dance, Guerrero’s outlook towards life is less based on vibes. “I think it’s important to go with the flow but I do appreciate structure. I’ll let things happen in a natural way but when it comes to choosing which people to keep in my immediate circle, carving out a space I can be comfortable in, making my own schedule, and having a say in my recent projects, I want to be more conscious now.”
Influencers may find it hard to strike a balance between the personal and public-facing, especially when every moment can be monetized. But Guerrero has never felt the need to follow any trends, or cave to the demands of the majority. “I think it’s easy to get caught up in what people expect of me, but in the end, I always do what feels right for me,” she says. “I want to stay true to who I am.”
Even though her career is pretty much in full force, Guerrero has no plans of letting her personal goals take the backseat. Some of the items on her bucket list for the year? Going to Coachella; exploring Paris; and meeting the likes of Tyla and Jungkook.
Of course, as someone who grew up in the public eye, she also strives to attain simple joys, such as traveling with her close group of friends. “I never got to have sleepovers growing up, so when my friends and I went to Japan and stayed in the same Airbnb, it was the closest I had ever gotten to that experience,” she says. “I loved shopping the whole day and getting home and doing little hauls with them. It was so memorable for me.”
I ask her if there’s anything jarring about having the entire archive of her life available online for public viewing, but she’s never seen it that way.
“I’m grateful that people have seen different versions of me over the years,” Niana Guerrero says. “And though my interests and style and mindset will evolve, I’ll grow and document as I go.”

Vanessa Lopes Ramalho[1] (born July 5, 2001)[2] is a Brazilian digital influencer and dancer, known for having more than 30.5 million followers on TikTok, where she is successful with her choreographies.[3][4] In 2024, she was a participant in the twenty-fourth edition of the reality show Big Brother Brasil; Vanessa's participation was brief and generated controversy.[5][6]
Biography
[edit]Lopes was born in Brasília, but moved to Recife as a child. She created a TikTok account while she was at university and, during the COVID-19 pandemic, started recording and posting dance videos on the app. As of January 2024, Lopes has 30.2 million followers on TikTok and 14.3 million followers on Instagram. She presents the podcast Não é TPM with Fernanda Schneider, Gabriela Mag, Victória Collen, Isa Paoli and Vivi Wanderley.[7][8]
In 2024, Vanessa Lopes was a member of the "Celebrity" group in the 24th season of Big Brother Brasil. In January of the same year, her TikTok account had a total of 1 billion likes.[9][10]
Personal life
[edit]Relationships and personal interests
[edit]Vanessa Lopes is openly bisexual.[11][12] In June 2021, she began dating football player and TikToker Ricardo Rêgo, which lasted six months. Vanessa also had involvement with actor João Guilherme,[13] and publicly shared interactions with other personalities, such as Luísa Sonza,[14] Lara Silva, Gabi Lopes and Gabriel Medina.[15][16]
On social media, Lopes also highlights her passion for sports, being a Flamengo[17][18] fan and a footvolley player,[19] as well as demonstrating an interest in surfing, an activity she also does during her free time.[20]
Accident
[edit]After completing high school, Lopes had the desire to go on exchange and study abroad. However, during a trip with a friend, DJ Alan Maciel, she was hit by a driver who fled the scene, near Porto de Galinhas. They were on their way to a show when their vehicle had a flat tire. At the time of the exchange, a car hit them and threw them about 20 meters away. Vanessa was holding the flashlight so that Maciel could have a better view when changing the tire.[21] At the time of the accident, Vanessa was just 18 years old, and this traumatic experience made her rethink the idea of living far from family and friends, leading her to conclude that it wasn't worth going abroad.[22]
A year after the road tragedy, Lopes decided to split her time between attending college for marketing and getting involved in creating digital content.[23]

### The Rise of Charli D'Amelio on TikTok

In the ever-evolving landscape of social media, Charli D'Amelio has become a beacon of fame, captivating audiences with her electrifying dance moves and charismatic personality. As the most popular TikTok dancer mentioned in the context, Charli D'Amelio has transformed the platform into a global phenomenon, with millions of followers around the world. 

#### The Journey to TikTok Stardom

Charli D'Amelio's journey to TikTok stardom began in 2017 when she started posting short videos on the platform. Unlike many other creators, she quickly found her niche with her unique style of dance and upbeat music videos. Her videos, which often featured her bouncing on a trampoline, quickly gained traction and she was soon signed to a record label.

#### The Popularity Boom

Charli's rise to fame on TikTok has been nothing short of meteoric. Within just a few months, she had amassed over 10 million followers, a feat that would have been unimaginable for many other TikTok creators. Her videos, which typically have a length of around 15 seconds, often go viral and are shared millions of times. This viral popularity has not only propelled her to fame but has also opened doors for her in various industries.

#### Beyond TikTok

While Charli D'Amelio's success on TikTok has been immense, her influence extends far beyond the platform. She has launched her own clothing line, collaborated with brands like Adidas and Nike, and even started her own reality TV show. Her ventures in the fashion and entertainment industries have further cemented her status as one of the most influential figures on social media.

#### Conclusion

Charli D'Amelio's journey from a TikTok dancer to a global celebrity is a testament to the power of creativity and perseverance. Her ability to capture the hearts and imaginations of millions on the platform has set her apart and has inspired countless others to follow their own dreams. As the most popular TikTok dancer mentioned in the context, Charli D'Amelio continues to lead the way, proving that with hard work and a bit of luck, anyone can achieve greatness on social media.
