Los Angeles, CA is a city known for its entertainment, beaches, and nightlife. While there are many activities to do in the City of Angels, you may have the urge to escape the city borders to explore something new. There are many unique day trips you can take – whether a longer trip to a national park or a shorter trip to an amusement park. Any of which are sure to pique your interest. To help you get started, we compiled a list of the 10 best day trips from Los Angeles. Keep reading to see what trips made the list.
1. Coronado, CA
Approximate distance: 130 miles
Estimated travel time: 3 hours
Just 3 hours and 130 miles south of Los Angeles lies Coronado, CA, a beautiful resort city located across the Big Bay from downtown San Diego, CA. Coronado, a name derived from the Coronado Islands, bears the nickname, “The Crown City.” There are many activities to do in Coronado such as visiting the USS Midway Museum, lounging at Coronado Beach, or going boating along the bay. If you find yourself wanting to stay for the weekend, book a room at the Hotel del Coronado, the second largest wooden structure in the United States.
2. Joshua Tree National Park
Approximate distance: 130 miles
Estimated travel time: 3 hours
Known for its distinct plants and starry nights, there is no shortage of adventure at Joshua Tree National Park. The park comprises two desert ecosystems, the Mojave and Colorado, and encompasses about 790,000 acres making it the second-largest national park in California, second only to Death Valley National Park. There are many things to do at Joshua Tree such as trying out the various climbing routes, hiking the many trails like the Arch Rock Nature Trail and Ryan Mountain Trail; or taking in the views at Barker Dam. It takes approximately 3 hours to get to Joshua Tree National Park so make sure to wake up early for this day trip from Los Angeles.
3. San Diego, CA
Approximate distance: 120 miles
Estimated travel time: 3 hours
If you are looking for some fun and excitement take a trip to San Diego, CA. Located roughly 3 hours east of Los Angeles, San Diego, CA is known as, “America’s Finest City” with its beautiful beaches and wonderful weather. The city lies along the Pacific Ocean and has unique typography filled with canyons, valleys, and mesas. If you head out to San Diego, be sure to explore the San Diego Zoo where you can see more than 650 species; Balboa Park, a historic cultural park with gardens, open spaces, and walking trails; and La Jolla Cove, a beautiful beach with surrounding cliffs.
4. San Gabriel Mountains National Monument
Approximate distance: 50 miles
Estimated travel time: 2 hours
San Gabriel Mountains National Monument spans over 340,000 miles and holds 600 archeological sites. It’s comprised of four different wilderness areas – San Gabriel, Sheep Mountain, Magic Mountain, and Pleasant View Ridge. San Gabriel Mountains National Monument is located about 2 hours and 50 miles east of Los Angeles making it a quick day trip from this city. When at San Gabriel Mountains National Monument you can do many different outdoor activities like hiking, cross-country skiing, and hunting.
5. Palm Springs, CA
Approximate distance: 100 miles
Estimated travel time: 1 hour and 50 minutes
If you are looking for fun in the sun consider checking out Palm Springs, CA. Palm Springs is considered the golf capital of the world and is located about 100 miles east of Los Angeles. You can get to Palm Springs, CA in about 1 hour and 50 minutes. A couple of activities to try out include golfing at Pete Dye Mountain Course, Desert Willow, or Escena Golf Club; watching tennis at the BNP Paribas Open, or exploring the Living Desert Zoo and Garden. With the diversity of activities, it’s no wonder why Palm Springs is considered one of the best day trips from Los Angeles.
6. Santa Catalina Island
Approximate distance: 50 miles
Estimated travel time: 1 hour
Located nearly 50 miles West of Los Angeles, Santa Catalina Island lies just off the Pacific Coast of California and is a favorite destination for boaters, adventurers, and tourists alike. A couple of activities to try out in Santa Catalina include lounging at Moonstone Beach, taking a tour of Avalon Theater, or visiting Catalina Museum for Art & History. Make sure to account for around one hour boat ride to Santa Catalina Island.
7. Tijuana, MX
Approximate distance: 220 miles
Estimated travel time: 3.5 hours
Located about 3 hours and 30 minutes from Los Angeles, the town of Tijuana, MX is known for its bullfighting and racetracks. In fact, Tijuana has one of the only seaside bullrings in the world, only second in size to Plaza México. Some things to check out in Tijuana include picking produce at the El Popo Market, checking out Avenida Revolucion, or walking along Tijuana’s scenic beaches.
8. Big Bear Lake
Approximate distance: 120 miles
Estimated travel time: 3 hours
Around 3 hours and 120 miles east of Los Angeles, Big Bear Lake, CA provides access to a ton of outdoor activities such as skiing, hiking, paddleboarding, and jet skiing. The city sits along a large fish-filled lake and is surrounded by beautiful pine trees of the San Bernardino National Forest. Many people go to Big Bear Lake to go skiing at Bear Mountain Ski Resort, visit animals at Big Bear Alpine Zoo, or hike Castle Rock trail. For an unforgettable experience, try to visit one of the many year-round events held at Big Bear like the Fishing for 50k Trout Derby or Big Bear Lake Oktoberfest.
9. Disneyland
Approximate distance: 30 miles
Estimated travel time: 30 minutes
If you want to try delicious food, love entertaining shows, or want to experience magic, this day trip is for you. Known as The Happiest Place of Earth, Disneyland is roughly 30 miles southeast of Los Angeles located in Anaheim, CA. Disneyland is full of fun activities for people of all ages. You can take pictures in front of the Magic Castle, ride Space Mountain, and travel up the Matterhorn. Make sure to wake up early for this day trip from Los Angeles as crowds can fill up quickly, especially during the weekends.
10. Solvang, CA
Approximate distance: 130 miles
Estimated travel time: 2 hours
If the idea of shopping at small businesses, going wine sampling, or strolling through a village sounds fun to you, then take a day trip to Solvang, CA. Situated 130 miles and nearly 2 hours northwest of Los Angeles, Solvang, CA is a historic Danish town that you’ll never get bored exploring. Some favorite things to see are the Little Mermaid statue and the historic church of Old Mission Santa Ines. You can also visit the town during an annual event like Solvang Stomp held in October or Danish Days held in September.

Los Angeles is already one of those places everyone’s heard about. But what really makes LA extra fun are all the tours and easy day trips you can add to your plans. There’s always a new corner to check out in the city or a quick escape just outside of it. That’s what makes exploring LA feel like a new adventure every time. Here, I’ve made a list of all the top tours and day trips you can take while in LA.
In a Hurry? Here Are Our Top 4 Los Angeles Tours and Day Trips Picks
Before We Escape…
While you most definitely can let your inner, spontaneous adventurer self out, taking trips are supposed to be relaxing (unless, you want the adrenaline rush of traveling unprepared, because kudos to you then). I highly recommend booking the things you need to book in advance. This includes tickets and admission fees.
You can also join organized day trips for a more relaxed experience. Some of the tours offer multiple stops that I recommend here, so it’ll be killing two, or more, birds with one stone.
Warner Bros. Studio Tour Hollywood
Best For: Behind-the-scenes movie magic, set tours, classic TV nostalgia
If you’re curious about how movies and TV shows come to life, I think the Warner Bros. Studio Tour is a must-do day trip while you’re in Los Angeles. It’s one of the best ways to get an insider’s look at real working sets, soundstages, and iconic filming locations. Located in Burbank, it’s about 20 minutes from central LA by car, so it’s super easy to fit into your itinerary.
One highlight is the Studio Tour itself. You’ll ride around the backlots where countless films and series have been shot, from classics like Friends to modern hits like The Big Bang Theory and Gilmore Girls. I also recommend spending time at Stage 48: Script to Screen, an interactive exhibit where you can sit on the famous Central Perk couch, see real costumes, and learn how a show is made from start to finish. If you’re a superhero fan, then definitely check out the DC Universe exhibit and the Batmobiles collection. And for Harry Potter fans, you can even get “sorted” into your Hogwarts House.
Getting There: A Classic Hollywood Tour in Los Angeles
It’s easy to visit Warner Bros. Studio on your own. Just book your Warner Bros. Studio Tour Hollywood tickets online in advance to secure your spot. You’ll join a small group and a guide to explore legendary backlots, soundstages, the famous Central Perk café, and behind-the-scenes movie magic.
The studio is in Burbank, about 20 minutes from central LA by car, with on-site parking available for a fee.
Quick Tips
- Book your studio tour tickets ahead of time. Popular time slots can sell out, especially on weekends and during holiday seasons.
- Bring a valid photo ID; you’ll need it to enter the studio.
- Large bags and filming on the tour are not allowed, but you can take photos at designated spots.
Santa Catalina Island
Best For: Island adventure, ocean views, laid-back coastal charm
Travel Time: ~2 hours from Los Angeles (including the ferry)
Just a short hop from LA, Catalina Island is like a whole new world. I think it’s one of the best day trips if you want to swap city streets for turquoise water and breezy island vibes. Catalina mixes SoCal cool with a touch of the Mediterranean, making it perfect for kayaking, snorkeling, or just soaking up Avalon’s harbor charm.
Out on the water, you can paddle through sea caves, snorkel in clear coves, or spot dolphins right from the ferry. Back on land, golf carts are the fun way to explore Avalon’s streets, hidden corners, and famous spots like the Catalina Casino. And if you’re a foodie, Catalina’s local bites are worth the trip alone. You can enjoy fresh seafood, sweets, and island history in one tasty stroll.
Getting There: A Coastal Day Trip from Los Angeles
Catalina is easy to reach. Just drive or rideshare to Long Beach and catch the Catalina Express ferry (this one’s from San Pedro to Avalon). Most people reach Avalon in about an hour once they’re onboard. I recommend booking tickets early, especially in summer or on weekends.
Once you’re there, there are some great ways to see the island. Out on the water, kayaking through sea caves is a must. Or you can stay dry but still see under the waves; I really recommend the Yellow Semi-Submarine tour. It’s quick, fun, and lets you watch schools of fish without getting wet.
Back in Avalon, golf carts are the way to explore. For the easiest adventure, I suggest booking this private guided golf cart tour. You’ll roll past the Catalina Casino, Pebbly Beach, and Wrigley Memorial with local stories along the way.
And if you’re craving local flavor, a food tour is the way to go. Taking a Catalina food tour is a tasty stroll along the waterfront with fresh seafood, sweets, and island history mixed in.
Quick Tips
- Bring layers. The ocean breeze can surprise you!
- Pack reef-safe sunscreen if you plan to snorkel or kayak.
- If you want to see dolphins, grab a seat on the ferry’s top deck for the best chance.
Joshua Tree National Park
Best For: Surreal desert scenery, rock formations, and stargazing
Travel Time: ~2.5–3 hours from Los Angeles
Just about 130 miles southeast of Los Angeles, Joshua Tree National Park is one of the best ways to trade city traffic for wide-open desert skies. I think it’s the perfect pick if you want to see a desert with strange, beautiful views: spiky Joshua trees, giant boulders, and sunsets that glow over the rocks.
The park’s otherworldly scenery is a dream for photographers and rock climbers alike. Even if you’re not into climbing cliffs, there are plenty of giant rock piles you can scramble up for fun and panoramic views. I suggest the Hidden Valley Trail for an easy, family-friendly 1-mile loop that shows off classic Joshua Tree sights. For more adventure, the 49 Palms Oasis Trail is a 3-mile trek to a surprise palm oasis tucked in the middle of the desert.
Getting There: A Desert Day Trip from Los Angeles
Start your adventure by either driving yourself or booking a tour that picks you up right from your hotel. It’s about a 2.5–3 hour drive from Los Angeles, so it’s totally doable as a day trip if you plan ahead.
If you’d rather not navigate on your own, I suggest this Joshua Tree National Park scenic tour. You’ll ride in a comfy van or an open-air Hummer with a small group and a guide who knows all the best viewpoints and geology stories. It’s perfect for families or first-time visitors who want an easy half-day escape.
For those who want to go at their own pace, try this self-guided driving audio tour. It follows a curated route with fun facts and hidden highlights along the way, plus a bonus stop at the Hidden Valley Nature Trail.
For adventure lovers, I recommend an off-road 4×4 tour that takes you deep into Joshua Tree’s rugged backcountry and lesser-seen valleys. Or you can try the open-air Hummer adventure, which adds a bit of thrill while you explore desert oases, spot wildlife, and snap photos of dramatic rock formations.
Quick Tips
- The drive takes approximately 2 hours and 45 minutes from LA, but plan for a full day (or longer) to truly appreciate what the park offers.
- Arrive early to beat both crowds and desert heat, especially during summer months.
Iconic Sights of Los Angeles Tour
Best For: First-timers, city highlights, classic LA photo ops
Travel Time: Full-day city tour (approx. 7–8 hours)
If you want to see all the highlights that make LA special in just one day, I think this full-day tour is a great choice. You’ll visit Hollywood’s Walk of Fame, the legendary Sunset Strip, the palm-lined streets of Beverly Hills, and the relaxed beaches around Santa Monica without the stress of planning every stop yourself.
Then, you can snap a photo at the Hollywood Sign, wander along Rodeo Drive, and soak up the ocean breeze at Venice Beach or the Santa Monica Pier. If you’re short on time, grouping a few highlights in one day is a fun way to get a good feel for what makes the city so iconic.
Getting There: A Must-Do City Tour in Los Angeles
Seeing LA’s biggest highlights can be tricky if you’re short on time. So, I recommend this full-day tour of the iconic sights of Los Angeles to make it easy. I really recommend it if you want to check off Hollywood, Beverly Hills, the Sunset Strip, Venice Beach, and Santa Monica Pier all in one day without the stress of driving or parking.
If you’re really tight on time, there’s also a half-day tour available. You’ll ride in an air-conditioned mini coach with a live guide, stop at top spots like the Hollywood Sign, Griffith Observatory, and Santa Monica Pier, and enjoy fun insider gossip along the way, plus audio guides in 11 languages if you depart from Hollywood.
Or, for the ultimate overview, I recommend the Grand City Tour of Los Angeles, Hollywood and Beverly Hills. It’s perfect if you want a comprehensive look at LA in one trip, with convenient hotel pickup, drop-off, and free time for lunch or shopping in between iconic stops.
Quick Tips
- Charge your phone. You’ll want it ready for snapping photos at all the famous spots, plus you might need maps or rideshare apps afterward.
- Plan for traffic. Even on a guided tour, LA traffic is real. Bring water, snacks, and something to keep you entertained while you’re on the road.
Malibu
Best For: Coastal road trips, iconic beaches, oceanfront dining
Travel Time: ~45 minutes from downtown Los Angeles (33 miles)
Just under an hour from LA, Malibu is a classic day trip when you want ocean views and beach vibes without going far. The Pacific Coast Highway alone is worth the drive. There are dramatic cliffs, hidden coves, and photo stops at every turn.
Malibu’s beaches are some of SoCal’s best. I recommend El Matador for sea caves and sunset shots, Zuma for wide open sand and swimming, and Malibu Lagoon for surf culture and celeb spotting. If you have extra time, hike scenic canyon trails, browse the Malibu Country Mart, or grab tacos and picnic right on the sand.
Getting There: A Seaside Day Trip from Los Angeles
Malibu is one of the easiest and most rewarding escapes from LA. Just jump on the Pacific Coast Highway and head west. In about 45 minutes, you’ll get ocean cliffs, beach pull-offs, and breezy coastal views make the drive part of the adventure.
If you’d rather let someone else handle the driving, you’ve got some great ways to explore. One good option is the Malibu: Exclusive Beautiful Beach and Celebrity Lifestyle Tour. You’ll ride in an open-air van, take in stories about Malibu’s celebrity history, and stop at classic spots like Malibu Pier, Point Dume’s ocean cliffs, and the Adamson House. You’ll also have time to browse the Malibu Country Mart for a snack or a quick shop.
For something more laid-back, this private vintage VW bus tour is a fun twist! It mixes local wine tasting with a mellow cruise through Malibu’s canyons and coastal roads. It’s definitely a relaxed way to see hidden lookouts and maybe spot some local wildlife along the way.
If you want to stretch your legs, I recommend the guided vineyard hike. It’s an easy loop through Malibu’s rolling hills with stops for local history and even a look at Chumash cave paintings. It wraps up with a couple cans of local wine to enjoy after your walk, which is a nice way to combine a bit of nature with something to sip.
Or, if you’re up for a bit of everything, try this Malibu Wine, Food & Beach Tour. It covers scenic roads, tucked-away nature preserves, and a stop at a private beach for photos. You’ll ride in an open-air bus with snacks and wine on board.
Quick Tips
- Leave early. The Pacific Coast Highway is beautiful but can get busy fast, especially on weekends.
- Bring layers and sunscreen. Pack a light jacket and plenty of sunblock.
Hollywood
Best For: Movie magic, famous landmarks, pop culture history
Travel Time: Right in the heart of Los Angeles
While Hollywood pops up in most city tours, this spotlight trip is all about soaking in everything that makes Tinseltown iconic. Hollywood is where LA’s movie magic really comes alive.
You can spend your day tracing the footsteps of legends at the TCL Chinese Theatre, hunting for your favorite stars on the boulevard, or even catching a glimpse of the Hollywood Sign perched above it all. If you love old-school glamour mixed with pop culture, a deep dive into Hollywood’s streets, studios, and behind-the-scenes stories is a must while you’re in LA.
Getting There: A Star-Studded Hollywood Tour in Los Angeles
One of the best things about exploring Hollywood is that you’re already in LA so no long drive is needed. Once you’re there, you can easily hop on a sightseeing tour or set out on foot to soak up the neighborhood’s most iconic spots.
For a fun overview without the parking headaches, I think an open-air bus is the way to go. The Hollywood open bus tours cruise past all the classics like the Walk of Fame, Dolby Theatre, Rodeo Drive, and those famous movie star homes you’ve always heard about. If you’d like a mix of Beverly Hills mansions and Hollywood landmarks, there’s also this Hollywood and Celebrity Homes Bus Tour hits the highlights and keeps an eye out for celebrity sightings too. There’s also the same tour plus Beverly Hills, but this time on an open air bus.
But if you’d rather explore on foot (and get closer to that iconic sign), I recommend lacing up for this Hollywood Sign Tour with comedians & their dogs. It is a unique experience! It’s a guided walk through Griffith Park with plenty of laughs, history, and epic skyline views. Or go all in on a classic LA bucket list moment with the original 2.5-Hour Hollywood sign hike, which gets you as close as possible to the sign (and helps you snap those envy-inducing shots without getting lost in the hills).
Quick Tips
- Bring water and sunscreen if you’re doing a hike. Griffith Park gets hot, especially midday.
- Keep cash handy for quick snacks or small souvenirs along Hollywood Boulevard.
- If you’re hoping to spot a celeb, hang out near trendy cafes or head up to the hills. You never know who you’ll see!
Griffith Observatory
Best For: Skyline views, stargazing, classic LA scenery
Travel Time: ~20–30 minutes from downtown Los Angeles
Perched high above the city in Griffith Park, Griffith Observatory is one of LA’s most beloved landmarks for good reason. It’s where locals and visitors alike come to soak up sweeping views of the city skyline, the Hollywood Sign, and the endless SoCal sunsets that make this spot a must.
Once you step inside, check out the free space exhibits, peer through historic telescopes, or catch a live show in the Samuel Oschin Planetarium. If you’re more into fresh air than star charts, the trails around the observatory lead to some of the best lookout points in LA. It’s perfect for snapping skyline photos or just soaking up that classic Southern California sunset.
Getting There: A Breathtaking Tour in Los Angeles
Griffith Observatory is just a quick drive from downtown Los Angeles, but part of the fun is getting there, especially if you love a good view along the way. Parking at the top can get tight on busy days, so a lot of visitors combine their trip with a scenic hike through Griffith Park instead.
One of the best ways to do it is on a guided walk, like this guided hiking tour through Griffith Park up towards the observatory. You’ll follow an expert local guide along a 3.5-mile route through the Hollywood Hills, learn fun bits of LA history, and get those must-have photos of the Hollywood Sign. The hike ends right at the Observatory, so you can explore inside or just relax and take in the sweeping skyline views. Morning and sunset departures mean you can pick your favorite vibe, be it golden light or city lights!
Quick Tips
- Bring a light jacket as it can get breezy up at the Observatory, especially after sunset.
- The planetarium shows aren’t free. Check the schedule and grab tickets early if you want to catch one.
- Stay after dark if you can! Telescopes on the lawn offer free public viewing on clear nights.
Big Bear Lake
Best For: Mountain escapes, fresh alpine air, year-round outdoor fun
Travel Time: ~2 hours from downtown Los Angeles
Just two hours from the bustle of Los Angeles, Big Bear Lake sits high in the San Bernardino Mountains at over 6,700 feet. This alpine village feels like a world away, with cool mountain breezes and pine forests that offer a refreshing break from the city’s heat.
Big Bear is fun to visit any time of year. In summer, rent a boat and spend time on the water. When spring arrives, the hills bloom with colorful wildflowers. Fall brings bright leaves and crisp air, while winter turns the area into a snowy playground for skiing and snow fun. Even though it’s so close to the city, it has completely different vibes that you will like if you’ve had enough of the bustle of LA.
Getting There: A Scenic Mountain Day Trip from Los Angeles
Reaching Big Bear Lake from Los Angeles is pretty straightforward. Most visitors take Highway 330 or Highway 18, winding through scenic mountain roads with sweeping views of the San Bernardino National Forest. It’s about a two-hour drive, but plan extra time to stop at overlooks or snap photos along the way.
Once you’re up there, you don’t have to stick to the usual trails or crowded spots. For something fun and local-approved, I recommend trying this locals’ favorite hike with lake swimming experience. You’ll get a short guided hike through the forest and then cool off at a secret swimming dock. It’s really the kind of hidden perk you’d only find with a local.
Or if you’d rather keep things laid-back, you can combine the mountain views with a little gourmet twist on the with this Big Bear Lake jeep tour with light lunch. It’s part scenic ride, part storytelling session, and ends with a stylish pop-up picnic in a forest spot known mostly to locals. It’s perfect for a quiet lunch surrounded by fresh mountain air.
Quick Tips
- Check the weather. It can change fast in the mountains.
- Fill up on gas early. There aren’t many gas stations up in Big Bear, so top off before you start driving up the mountain roads.
- Take it slow on the roads. The mountain highways are beautiful but winding. Drive carefully and enjoy the views along the way.
More Fun Little Adventures Around Los Angeles
Echo Park Swan Boats
If you feel like swapping the city noise for something chill, I think paddling a swan boat around Echo Park Lake is a cute idea. It’s easy, affordable, and you can pick daytime or even go at night when the skyline’s all lit up. Nice way to just float, talk, and enjoy a break.
Ultimate LA Bike Tour
For something more active, you might like this full-day bike ride through West Hollywood, Beverly Hills, Santa Monica, and Venice. I like that it mixes cycling with little stories, celeb house sightings, and a stop at Greystone Mansion. It’s a fun way to cover a lot of ground without feeling rushed.
Universal Studios Hollywood: VIP Tour
If you’re into theme parks but hate standing in line all day, this VIP Universal pass could be worth it. You skip the lines, get a behind-the-scenes peek at real movie sets, and there’s even valet parking and a good meal thrown in. Not bad if you want to make the most of your day there.
Your Perfect LA Escape Awaits
Before you head out, keep a few things in mind to make the most of your LA day trips. Always check the weather, pack layers and sunscreen, and wear comfy shoes since you might hit a beach, a canyon, and a city street all in one day. If you’re driving, plan for traffic and parking fees, and start early when you can to avoid crowds.
It’s also worth keeping your energy up with some local bites. LA’s food scene is too good to skip! If you need ideas, I suggest browsing these famous Los Angeles foods for must-try eats along the way. And if you’re still building your plan, this list of things to do in Los Angeles can help round out your adventures. Enjoy exploring!

Table of Contents
Introduction
I woke up in my tiny Koreatown apartment, craving ocean air that didn’t smell like taco grease and Uber exhaust. By 7:15 a.m. I had a mug of cheap coffee, a half-charged phone, and enough gas to get somewhere—anywhere—before the 405 turned into a parking lot. These five day trips from los angeles saved my sanity over the past year; each one fits into a single Saturday, costs less than a Disneyland churro stand, and gives you bragging rights that don’t involve filtering selfies at the Hollywood sign.
Santa Barbara: ninety minutes to fake European bliss
The 101 north is a straight shot, but I still manage to miss the exit every time. Roll down the windows around Ventura and the air turns salty; by the time you hit Santa Barbara the temperature drops five degrees and your playlist suddenly feels more sophisticated. Park at East Beach lot ($2.25 per hour, card accepted) and walk the palm-lined path toward Stearns Wharf. I once saw a pelican steal a toddler’s sandwich here—equal parts horrifying and hilarious.
Almond croissants and hidden courtyards
I follow the same route each visit: croissant at Renaud’s (still warm, flaky enough to ruin your shirt), then a wander up State Street until the tilework of the old courthouse appears. If you’re building a bucket-list of single-day escapes, my Top Bucket List Travel Destinations You Can Explore in a Single Day guide rounds up global spots you can steal. I follow the same route each visit: croissant at Renaud’s (still warm, flaky enough to ruin your shirt), then a wander up State Street until the tilework of the old courthouse appears. Climb the tower—free, no line—and you’ll see red-tile roofs crammed between mountains and sea. Later I cut over to Anapamu Street, duck into the public library’s back garden, and pretend I’m in a Spanish novella for twenty minutes. No tour bus stops here; that’s the point.
Cheap wine without the side-eye
Santa Barbara’s Urban Wine Trail sounds bougie until you realize most tasting rooms pour for $10 and waive the fee if you buy a bottle. My go-to is Riverbench on Anacapa; their sparkling rosé tastes like strawberry Pop Rocks and the bartender lets you keep the glass. Dump the guilt, stash the glass in your trunk, and you’re back on the 101 before sunset traffic spawns.
Joshua Tree: where your phone gives up and you remember what stars look like
Two hours east and the city dissolves into wind farms, then boulder fields that feel like a Dr. Seuss fever dream. I always stop at the Joshua Tree Visitor Center for a map—even though the loop roads are basically a figure eight—because the ranger behind the counter gives free coffee refills to anyone carrying a reusable cup. If you ever flip the map to the desert north-east, my Unforgettable Day Trips from Las Vegas guide covers sun-to-snow routes in the same timeframe. Pro tip: bring the cup.
Hidden Valley loop before the crowds
I hit Hidden Valley Trail at sunrise; the parking lot has three cars max and the rocks glow pink. The loop is only one mile, but you’ll spend forty minutes photographing cacti and trying not to step on lizards. I once watched a guy propose here—she said yes, then immediately asked if there was cell service. (There isn’t.)
Keys View for the price of nothing
Drive another twenty minutes up the ridge and you’ll stare down the Coachella Valley from 5,185 feet. On clear winter days you can see the Salton Sea shimmering like a broken mirror. I sat on the stone wall until my fingers went numb, listening to nothing but wind and the occasional raven. That’s the real luxury—silence you don’t have to pay for.
Date shakes and gas-station art
Leave the park through the west entrance, pull into the funky strip of cabins that calls itself Joshua Tree town. Crossroads Café serves a date shake thick enough to stand a straw upright; I always add a shot of espresso because caffeine in the desert feels poetic. Next door, the thrift store has a wall of VHS tapes for a dollar each—buy one, even if you don’t own a VCR. It’s a souvenir that weighs nothing and sparks conversations.
Malibu: forty-five minutes to feel like a celebrity on a budget
Take the PCH north past Topanga and the cliffs drop into the ocean so fast your ears pop. I usually exit at Las Flores Canyon, park for free along the shoulder, and hike the paved path down to El Matador State Beach. The descent is steep enough to make your calves hate you, but the sea arches at the bottom photograph like a Greek island—no filter, no crowds before 10 a.m.
Sea caves and wet sneakers
Time the tide right (check the chart online) and you can duck into a cave that opens onto a hidden pocket of sand. I once found a message in a plastic bottle here: a kid’s drawing of a dinosaur and the words “be happy.” I left it there; the next person deserves the smile too.
Neptune’s Net: biker bar, surfer cafeteria, your lunch
Cross back over the highway and you’ll hit Neptune’s Net, all neon beer signs and Harley exhaust. Order the clam chowder bread bowl; it’s $12, tastes like salt and nostalgia, and the cashier doesn’t care if you show up in flip-flops or Ferragamo. Sit on the upper deck, watch the Pacific glitter, and try to count how many different languages you hear. I stopped at seven. Prefer palm trees to fog? Check my Ultimate San Francisco Day Trips guide for Nor-Cal ocean-to-redwood escapes too.
Big Bear Lake: two-and-a-half hours to fake winter when L.A. is still sweating
Climb the 330 through Running Springs and the temperature drops a degree every mile. I roll the windows down just to smell pine instead of brake dust. By the time the lake appears—frozen edges in January, glassy blue in July—I’ve already forgotten what freeway rage feels like.
Village Rim Trail for the lazy hiker
No skis? No problem. Park at the Discovery Center, grab a free map, and walk the Village Rim Trail. It’s mostly flat, hugs the shoreline, and delivers postcard views without the elevation guilt. I saw a bald eagle here last March; everyone else was taking selfies at the ski resort parking lot.
Coffee that doesn’t taste like campfire
Amangela’s sits above a bike shop that rents fat-tire cycles for snow. Their blueberry cornmeal muffin is the size of a softball and pairs perfectly with a honey-lavender latte. I always grab an extra muffin for the drive down—it’s gone before I hit the first switchback.
Alpine slide and alpine guilt
If you’re visiting summer-through-fall, the Alpine Slide at Magic Mountain is worth the $20. You ride a plastic sled down a concrete chute, wind in your face, lake expanding below. I screamed the entire way; the eight-year-old behind me did not. Humbling.
Solvang – Denmark without the jet-lag (2 hrs north-west)
Exit the 101 at Buellton, follow the smell of fresh waffles, and suddenly you’re in a Hans Christian Andersen pop-up book. Windmills spin, half-timbered houses lean at impossible angles, and every bakery pumps out almond-scented steam. I park on Copenhagen Drive—three free hours if you feed the meter quarters you found under the seat.
Kringle and Viking selfies
Mortensen’s Bakery has a tray of almond kringle that sells out by 11 a.m. I buy one still warm, eat it on the wooden bench outside, and pretend the calories don’t count on vacation days. Across the street, the giant red clog begs for a foot photo—obligatory, embrace the cliché.
Wine tasting that won’t bankrupt you
Walk two blocks south to Presidio Winery—tiny patio, string lights, laid-back bartender who pours four tastes for $8 and waves the fee if you post an Instagram story tagging them. Their sparkling brut is crisp enough to cut through kringle sugar; I left with two cans (yes, cans) because road-trip rules apply.
Quick comparison cheat-sheet
| Spot | Drive Time | Best Month | One Must-Eat | Parking Cash Needed |
| Santa Barbara | 90 min | Sept–May | Almond croissant | $8–15/day |
| Joshua Tree | 2 hrs | Oct–Apr | Date shake | $30 park fee |
| Malibu | 45 min | Year-round | Clam chowder bread | $10 shoulder |
| Big Bear | 2.5 hrs | Dec–Mar | Blueberry muffin | Free lots |
| Solvang | 2 hrs | Year-round | Almond kringle | Free 3 h |
Final reality check
You don’t need a private jet, a trust fund, or a three-day weekend. You need half a tank of gas, a Spotify playlist that doesn’t suck, and the guts to leave before sunrise. Every spot on this list I’ve done round-trip in under 12 hours, back home in time to shower, order Thai food, and sleep in my own bed. That’s the magic of day trips from los angeles: they feel like stolen time, not borrowed money.

**Los Angeles Day Trips: An Adventure in the Outdoors and Entertainment**

Los Angeles, the City of Angels, is not just a bustling metropolis; it's also a playground for adventure-seekers and nature lovers. With a wealth of day trips that can rival any city adventure, there's something for everyone to explore. Whether you're looking to escape the hustle and bustle of the city or simply seek out something new, Los Angeles offers a plethora of unique day trips that can be just as exciting as any city excursion.

**National Parks Day Trips**

Los Angeles is home to several national parks that offer breathtaking landscapes and a chance to disconnect from the city. Joshua Tree National Park, for instance, is a gem nestled in the Mojave Desert, offering a surreal landscape of rock formations and desert wildflowers. Another gem is the Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks, where you can hike through towering sequoia groves and explore the Sierra Nevada mountains.

**Amusement Parks**

If you're looking for a more indulgent day trip, Los Angeles has a variety of amusement parks to choose from. Universal Studios Hollywood is a must-visit for fans of the Harry Potter franchise and offers a thrilling ride through the wizarding world. For a more traditional amusement park experience, Knott's Berry Farm in Anaheim is a favorite among families. Both parks offer thrilling rides, delicious food, and a chance to experience the magic of America's entertainment capital.

**Exploring the Outdoors**

Los Angeles is also a gateway to the great outdoors, with nearby national parks and scenic drives offering plenty of adventure. The Angeles National Forest, located just a few hours from Los Angeles, is a paradise for hikers and nature enthusiasts. Drive up to the San Gabriel Mountains or head south to the San Bernardino National Forest, where you can explore the rugged beauty of the Sierra Nevada.

**Conclusion**

Los Angeles is more than just a city; it's a gateway to a world of adventure and exploration. Whether you're seeking a day trip to a nearby national park or a longer adventure to an amusement park, Los Angeles offers something for everyone. So pack your bags and get ready for a day filled with excitement, adventure, and unforgettable memories.

Los Angeles, CA is a city known for its entertainment, beaches, and nightlife. While there are many activities to do in the City of Angels, you may have the urge to escape the city borders to explore something new. There are many unique day trips you can take – whether a longer trip to a national park or a shorter trip to an amusement park. Any of which are sure to pique your interest. To help you get started, we compiled a list of the 10 best day trips from Los Angeles. Keep reading to see what trips made the list.
1. Coronado, CA
Approximate distance: 130 miles
Estimated travel time: 3 hours
Just 3 hours and 130 miles south of Los Angeles lies Coronado, CA, a beautiful resort city located across the Big Bay from downtown San Diego, CA. Coronado, a name derived from the Coronado Islands, bears the nickname, “The Crown City.” There are many activities to do in Coronado such as visiting the USS Midway Museum, lounging at Coronado Beach, or going boating along the bay. If you find yourself wanting to stay for the weekend, book a room at the Hotel del Coronado, the second largest wooden structure in the United States.
2. Joshua Tree National Park
Approximate distance: 130 miles
Estimated travel time: 3 hours
Known for its distinct plants and starry nights, there is no shortage of adventure at Joshua Tree National Park. The park comprises two desert ecosystems, the Mojave and Colorado, and encompasses about 790,000 acres making it the second-largest national park in California, second only to Death Valley National Park. There are many things to do at Joshua Tree such as trying out the various climbing routes, hiking the many trails like the Arch Rock Nature Trail and Ryan Mountain Trail; or taking in the views at Barker Dam. It takes approximately 3 hours to get to Joshua Tree National Park so make sure to wake up early for this day trip from Los Angeles.
3. San Diego, CA
Approximate distance: 120 miles
Estimated travel time: 3 hours
If you are looking for some fun and excitement take a trip to San Diego, CA. Located roughly 3 hours east of Los Angeles, San Diego, CA is known as, “America’s Finest City” with its beautiful beaches and wonderful weather. The city lies along the Pacific Ocean and has unique typography filled with canyons, valleys, and mesas. If you head out to San Diego, be sure to explore the San Diego Zoo where you can see more than 650 species; Balboa Park, a historic cultural park with gardens, open spaces, and walking trails; and La Jolla Cove, a beautiful beach with surrounding cliffs.
4. San Gabriel Mountains National Monument
Approximate distance: 50 miles
Estimated travel time: 2 hours
San Gabriel Mountains National Monument spans over 340,000 miles and holds 600 archeological sites. It’s comprised of four different wilderness areas – San Gabriel, Sheep Mountain, Magic Mountain, and Pleasant View Ridge. San Gabriel Mountains National Monument is located about 2 hours and 50 miles east of Los Angeles making it a quick day trip from this city. When at San Gabriel Mountains National Monument you can do many different outdoor activities like hiking, cross-country skiing, and hunting.
5. Palm Springs, CA
Approximate distance: 100 miles
Estimated travel time: 1 hour and 50 minutes
If you are looking for fun in the sun consider checking out Palm Springs, CA. Palm Springs is considered the golf capital of the world and is located about 100 miles east of Los Angeles. You can get to Palm Springs, CA in about 1 hour and 50 minutes. A couple of activities to try out include golfing at Pete Dye Mountain Course, Desert Willow, or Escena Golf Club; watching tennis at the BNP Paribas Open, or exploring the Living Desert Zoo and Garden. With the diversity of activities, it’s no wonder why Palm Springs is considered one of the best day trips from Los Angeles.
6. Santa Catalina Island
Approximate distance: 50 miles
Estimated travel time: 1 hour
Located nearly 50 miles West of Los Angeles, Santa Catalina Island lies just off the Pacific Coast of California and is a favorite destination for boaters, adventurers, and tourists alike. A couple of activities to try out in Santa Catalina include lounging at Moonstone Beach, taking a tour of Avalon Theater, or visiting Catalina Museum for Art & History. Make sure to account for around one hour boat ride to Santa Catalina Island.
7. Tijuana, MX
Approximate distance: 220 miles
Estimated travel time: 3.5 hours
Located about 3 hours and 30 minutes from Los Angeles, the town of Tijuana, MX is known for its bullfighting and racetracks. In fact, Tijuana has one of the only seaside bullrings in the world, only second in size to Plaza México. Some things to check out in Tijuana include picking produce at the El Popo Market, checking out Avenida Revolucion, or walking along Tijuana’s scenic beaches.
8. Big Bear Lake
Approximate distance: 120 miles
Estimated travel time: 3 hours
Around 3 hours and 120 miles east of Los Angeles, Big Bear Lake, CA provides access to a ton of outdoor activities such as skiing, hiking, paddleboarding, and jet skiing. The city sits along a large fish-filled lake and is surrounded by beautiful pine trees of the San Bernardino National Forest. Many people go to Big Bear Lake to go skiing at Bear Mountain Ski Resort, visit animals at Big Bear Alpine Zoo, or hike Castle Rock trail. For an unforgettable experience, try to visit one of the many year-round events held at Big Bear like the Fishing for 50k Trout Derby or Big Bear Lake Oktoberfest.
9. Disneyland
Approximate distance: 30 miles
Estimated travel time: 30 minutes
If you want to try delicious food, love entertaining shows, or want to experience magic, this day trip is for you. Known as The Happiest Place of Earth, Disneyland is roughly 30 miles southeast of Los Angeles located in Anaheim, CA. Disneyland is full of fun activities for people of all ages. You can take pictures in front of the Magic Castle, ride Space Mountain, and travel up the Matterhorn. Make sure to wake up early for this day trip from Los Angeles as crowds can fill up quickly, especially during the weekends.
10. Solvang, CA
Approximate distance: 130 miles
Estimated travel time: 2 hours
If the idea of shopping at small businesses, going wine sampling, or strolling through a village sounds fun to you, then take a day trip to Solvang, CA. Situated 130 miles and nearly 2 hours northwest of Los Angeles, Solvang, CA is a historic Danish town that you’ll never get bored exploring. Some favorite things to see are the Little Mermaid statue and the historic church of Old Mission Santa Ines. You can also visit the town during an annual event like Solvang Stomp held in October or Danish Days held in September.

Los Angeles is already one of those places everyone’s heard about. But what really makes LA extra fun are all the tours and easy day trips you can add to your plans. There’s always a new corner to check out in the city or a quick escape just outside of it. That’s what makes exploring LA feel like a new adventure every time. Here, I’ve made a list of all the top tours and day trips you can take while in LA.
In a Hurry? Here Are Our Top 4 Los Angeles Tours and Day Trips Picks
Before We Escape…
While you most definitely can let your inner, spontaneous adventurer self out, taking trips are supposed to be relaxing (unless, you want the adrenaline rush of traveling unprepared, because kudos to you then). I highly recommend booking the things you need to book in advance. This includes tickets and admission fees.
You can also join organized day trips for a more relaxed experience. Some of the tours offer multiple stops that I recommend here, so it’ll be killing two, or more, birds with one stone.
Warner Bros. Studio Tour Hollywood
Best For: Behind-the-scenes movie magic, set tours, classic TV nostalgia
If you’re curious about how movies and TV shows come to life, I think the Warner Bros. Studio Tour is a must-do day trip while you’re in Los Angeles. It’s one of the best ways to get an insider’s look at real working sets, soundstages, and iconic filming locations. Located in Burbank, it’s about 20 minutes from central LA by car, so it’s super easy to fit into your itinerary.
One highlight is the Studio Tour itself. You’ll ride around the backlots where countless films and series have been shot, from classics like Friends to modern hits like The Big Bang Theory and Gilmore Girls. I also recommend spending time at Stage 48: Script to Screen, an interactive exhibit where you can sit on the famous Central Perk couch, see real costumes, and learn how a show is made from start to finish. If you’re a superhero fan, then definitely check out the DC Universe exhibit and the Batmobiles collection. And for Harry Potter fans, you can even get “sorted” into your Hogwarts House.
Getting There: A Classic Hollywood Tour in Los Angeles
It’s easy to visit Warner Bros. Studio on your own. Just book your Warner Bros. Studio Tour Hollywood tickets online in advance to secure your spot. You’ll join a small group and a guide to explore legendary backlots, soundstages, the famous Central Perk café, and behind-the-scenes movie magic.
The studio is in Burbank, about 20 minutes from central LA by car, with on-site parking available for a fee.
Quick Tips
- Book your studio tour tickets ahead of time. Popular time slots can sell out, especially on weekends and during holiday seasons.
- Bring a valid photo ID; you’ll need it to enter the studio.
- Large bags and filming on the tour are not allowed, but you can take photos at designated spots.
Santa Catalina Island
Best For: Island adventure, ocean views, laid-back coastal charm
Travel Time: ~2 hours from Los Angeles (including the ferry)
Just a short hop from LA, Catalina Island is like a whole new world. I think it’s one of the best day trips if you want to swap city streets for turquoise water and breezy island vibes. Catalina mixes SoCal cool with a touch of the Mediterranean, making it perfect for kayaking, snorkeling, or just soaking up Avalon’s harbor charm.
Out on the water, you can paddle through sea caves, snorkel in clear coves, or spot dolphins right from the ferry. Back on land, golf carts are the fun way to explore Avalon’s streets, hidden corners, and famous spots like the Catalina Casino. And if you’re a foodie, Catalina’s local bites are worth the trip alone. You can enjoy fresh seafood, sweets, and island history in one tasty stroll.
Getting There: A Coastal Day Trip from Los Angeles
Catalina is easy to reach. Just drive or rideshare to Long Beach and catch the Catalina Express ferry (this one’s from San Pedro to Avalon). Most people reach Avalon in about an hour once they’re onboard. I recommend booking tickets early, especially in summer or on weekends.
Once you’re there, there are some great ways to see the island. Out on the water, kayaking through sea caves is a must. Or you can stay dry but still see under the waves; I really recommend the Yellow Semi-Submarine tour. It’s quick, fun, and lets you watch schools of fish without getting wet.
Back in Avalon, golf carts are the way to explore. For the easiest adventure, I suggest booking this private guided golf cart tour. You’ll roll past the Catalina Casino, Pebbly Beach, and Wrigley Memorial with local stories along the way.
And if you’re craving local flavor, a food tour is the way to go. Taking a Catalina food tour is a tasty stroll along the waterfront with fresh seafood, sweets, and island history mixed in.
Quick Tips
- Bring layers. The ocean breeze can surprise you!
- Pack reef-safe sunscreen if you plan to snorkel or kayak.
- If you want to see dolphins, grab a seat on the ferry’s top deck for the best chance.
Joshua Tree National Park
Best For: Surreal desert scenery, rock formations, and stargazing
Travel Time: ~2.5–3 hours from Los Angeles
Just about 130 miles southeast of Los Angeles, Joshua Tree National Park is one of the best ways to trade city traffic for wide-open desert skies. I think it’s the perfect pick if you want to see a desert with strange, beautiful views: spiky Joshua trees, giant boulders, and sunsets that glow over the rocks.
The park’s otherworldly scenery is a dream for photographers and rock climbers alike. Even if you’re not into climbing cliffs, there are plenty of giant rock piles you can scramble up for fun and panoramic views. I suggest the Hidden Valley Trail for an easy, family-friendly 1-mile loop that shows off classic Joshua Tree sights. For more adventure, the 49 Palms Oasis Trail is a 3-mile trek to a surprise palm oasis tucked in the middle of the desert.
Getting There: A Desert Day Trip from Los Angeles
Start your adventure by either driving yourself or booking a tour that picks you up right from your hotel. It’s about a 2.5–3 hour drive from Los Angeles, so it’s totally doable as a day trip if you plan ahead.
If you’d rather not navigate on your own, I suggest this Joshua Tree National Park scenic tour. You’ll ride in a comfy van or an open-air Hummer with a small group and a guide who knows all the best viewpoints and geology stories. It’s perfect for families or first-time visitors who want an easy half-day escape.
For those who want to go at their own pace, try this self-guided driving audio tour. It follows a curated route with fun facts and hidden highlights along the way, plus a bonus stop at the Hidden Valley Nature Trail.
For adventure lovers, I recommend an off-road 4×4 tour that takes you deep into Joshua Tree’s rugged backcountry and lesser-seen valleys. Or you can try the open-air Hummer adventure, which adds a bit of thrill while you explore desert oases, spot wildlife, and snap photos of dramatic rock formations.
Quick Tips
- The drive takes approximately 2 hours and 45 minutes from LA, but plan for a full day (or longer) to truly appreciate what the park offers.
- Arrive early to beat both crowds and desert heat, especially during summer months.
Iconic Sights of Los Angeles Tour
Best For: First-timers, city highlights, classic LA photo ops
Travel Time: Full-day city tour (approx. 7–8 hours)
If you want to see all the highlights that make LA special in just one day, I think this full-day tour is a great choice. You’ll visit Hollywood’s Walk of Fame, the legendary Sunset Strip, the palm-lined streets of Beverly Hills, and the relaxed beaches around Santa Monica without the stress of planning every stop yourself.
Then, you can snap a photo at the Hollywood Sign, wander along Rodeo Drive, and soak up the ocean breeze at Venice Beach or the Santa Monica Pier. If you’re short on time, grouping a few highlights in one day is a fun way to get a good feel for what makes the city so iconic.
Getting There: A Must-Do City Tour in Los Angeles
Seeing LA’s biggest highlights can be tricky if you’re short on time. So, I recommend this full-day tour of the iconic sights of Los Angeles to make it easy. I really recommend it if you want to check off Hollywood, Beverly Hills, the Sunset Strip, Venice Beach, and Santa Monica Pier all in one day without the stress of driving or parking.
If you’re really tight on time, there’s also a half-day tour available. You’ll ride in an air-conditioned mini coach with a live guide, stop at top spots like the Hollywood Sign, Griffith Observatory, and Santa Monica Pier, and enjoy fun insider gossip along the way, plus audio guides in 11 languages if you depart from Hollywood.
Or, for the ultimate overview, I recommend the Grand City Tour of Los Angeles, Hollywood and Beverly Hills. It’s perfect if you want a comprehensive look at LA in one trip, with convenient hotel pickup, drop-off, and free time for lunch or shopping in between iconic stops.
Quick Tips
- Charge your phone. You’ll want it ready for snapping photos at all the famous spots, plus you might need maps or rideshare apps afterward.
- Plan for traffic. Even on a guided tour, LA traffic is real. Bring water, snacks, and something to keep you entertained while you’re on the road.
Malibu
Best For: Coastal road trips, iconic beaches, oceanfront dining
Travel Time: ~45 minutes from downtown Los Angeles (33 miles)
Just under an hour from LA, Malibu is a classic day trip when you want ocean views and beach vibes without going far. The Pacific Coast Highway alone is worth the drive. There are dramatic cliffs, hidden coves, and photo stops at every turn.
Malibu’s beaches are some of SoCal’s best. I recommend El Matador for sea caves and sunset shots, Zuma for wide open sand and swimming, and Malibu Lagoon for surf culture and celeb spotting. If you have extra time, hike scenic canyon trails, browse the Malibu Country Mart, or grab tacos and picnic right on the sand.
Getting There: A Seaside Day Trip from Los Angeles
Malibu is one of the easiest and most rewarding escapes from LA. Just jump on the Pacific Coast Highway and head west. In about 45 minutes, you’ll get ocean cliffs, beach pull-offs, and breezy coastal views make the drive part of the adventure.
If you’d rather let someone else handle the driving, you’ve got some great ways to explore. One good option is the Malibu: Exclusive Beautiful Beach and Celebrity Lifestyle Tour. You’ll ride in an open-air van, take in stories about Malibu’s celebrity history, and stop at classic spots like Malibu Pier, Point Dume’s ocean cliffs, and the Adamson House. You’ll also have time to browse the Malibu Country Mart for a snack or a quick shop.
For something more laid-back, this private vintage VW bus tour is a fun twist! It mixes local wine tasting with a mellow cruise through Malibu’s canyons and coastal roads. It’s definitely a relaxed way to see hidden lookouts and maybe spot some local wildlife along the way.
If you want to stretch your legs, I recommend the guided vineyard hike. It’s an easy loop through Malibu’s rolling hills with stops for local history and even a look at Chumash cave paintings. It wraps up with a couple cans of local wine to enjoy after your walk, which is a nice way to combine a bit of nature with something to sip.
Or, if you’re up for a bit of everything, try this Malibu Wine, Food & Beach Tour. It covers scenic roads, tucked-away nature preserves, and a stop at a private beach for photos. You’ll ride in an open-air bus with snacks and wine on board.
Quick Tips
- Leave early. The Pacific Coast Highway is beautiful but can get busy fast, especially on weekends.
- Bring layers and sunscreen. Pack a light jacket and plenty of sunblock.
Hollywood
Best For: Movie magic, famous landmarks, pop culture history
Travel Time: Right in the heart of Los Angeles
While Hollywood pops up in most city tours, this spotlight trip is all about soaking in everything that makes Tinseltown iconic. Hollywood is where LA’s movie magic really comes alive.
You can spend your day tracing the footsteps of legends at the TCL Chinese Theatre, hunting for your favorite stars on the boulevard, or even catching a glimpse of the Hollywood Sign perched above it all. If you love old-school glamour mixed with pop culture, a deep dive into Hollywood’s streets, studios, and behind-the-scenes stories is a must while you’re in LA.
Getting There: A Star-Studded Hollywood Tour in Los Angeles
One of the best things about exploring Hollywood is that you’re already in LA so no long drive is needed. Once you’re there, you can easily hop on a sightseeing tour or set out on foot to soak up the neighborhood’s most iconic spots.
For a fun overview without the parking headaches, I think an open-air bus is the way to go. The Hollywood open bus tours cruise past all the classics like the Walk of Fame, Dolby Theatre, Rodeo Drive, and those famous movie star homes you’ve always heard about. If you’d like a mix of Beverly Hills mansions and Hollywood landmarks, there’s also this Hollywood and Celebrity Homes Bus Tour hits the highlights and keeps an eye out for celebrity sightings too. There’s also the same tour plus Beverly Hills, but this time on an open air bus.
But if you’d rather explore on foot (and get closer to that iconic sign), I recommend lacing up for this Hollywood Sign Tour with comedians & their dogs. It is a unique experience! It’s a guided walk through Griffith Park with plenty of laughs, history, and epic skyline views. Or go all in on a classic LA bucket list moment with the original 2.5-Hour Hollywood sign hike, which gets you as close as possible to the sign (and helps you snap those envy-inducing shots without getting lost in the hills).
Quick Tips
- Bring water and sunscreen if you’re doing a hike. Griffith Park gets hot, especially midday.
- Keep cash handy for quick snacks or small souvenirs along Hollywood Boulevard.
- If you’re hoping to spot a celeb, hang out near trendy cafes or head up to the hills. You never know who you’ll see!
Griffith Observatory
Best For: Skyline views, stargazing, classic LA scenery
Travel Time: ~20–30 minutes from downtown Los Angeles
Perched high above the city in Griffith Park, Griffith Observatory is one of LA’s most beloved landmarks for good reason. It’s where locals and visitors alike come to soak up sweeping views of the city skyline, the Hollywood Sign, and the endless SoCal sunsets that make this spot a must.
Once you step inside, check out the free space exhibits, peer through historic telescopes, or catch a live show in the Samuel Oschin Planetarium. If you’re more into fresh air than star charts, the trails around the observatory lead to some of the best lookout points in LA. It’s perfect for snapping skyline photos or just soaking up that classic Southern California sunset.
Getting There: A Breathtaking Tour in Los Angeles
Griffith Observatory is just a quick drive from downtown Los Angeles, but part of the fun is getting there, especially if you love a good view along the way. Parking at the top can get tight on busy days, so a lot of visitors combine their trip with a scenic hike through Griffith Park instead.
One of the best ways to do it is on a guided walk, like this guided hiking tour through Griffith Park up towards the observatory. You’ll follow an expert local guide along a 3.5-mile route through the Hollywood Hills, learn fun bits of LA history, and get those must-have photos of the Hollywood Sign. The hike ends right at the Observatory, so you can explore inside or just relax and take in the sweeping skyline views. Morning and sunset departures mean you can pick your favorite vibe, be it golden light or city lights!
Quick Tips
- Bring a light jacket as it can get breezy up at the Observatory, especially after sunset.
- The planetarium shows aren’t free. Check the schedule and grab tickets early if you want to catch one.
- Stay after dark if you can! Telescopes on the lawn offer free public viewing on clear nights.
Big Bear Lake
Best For: Mountain escapes, fresh alpine air, year-round outdoor fun
Travel Time: ~2 hours from downtown Los Angeles
Just two hours from the bustle of Los Angeles, Big Bear Lake sits high in the San Bernardino Mountains at over 6,700 feet. This alpine village feels like a world away, with cool mountain breezes and pine forests that offer a refreshing break from the city’s heat.
Big Bear is fun to visit any time of year. In summer, rent a boat and spend time on the water. When spring arrives, the hills bloom with colorful wildflowers. Fall brings bright leaves and crisp air, while winter turns the area into a snowy playground for skiing and snow fun. Even though it’s so close to the city, it has completely different vibes that you will like if you’ve had enough of the bustle of LA.
Getting There: A Scenic Mountain Day Trip from Los Angeles
Reaching Big Bear Lake from Los Angeles is pretty straightforward. Most visitors take Highway 330 or Highway 18, winding through scenic mountain roads with sweeping views of the San Bernardino National Forest. It’s about a two-hour drive, but plan extra time to stop at overlooks or snap photos along the way.
Once you’re up there, you don’t have to stick to the usual trails or crowded spots. For something fun and local-approved, I recommend trying this locals’ favorite hike with lake swimming experience. You’ll get a short guided hike through the forest and then cool off at a secret swimming dock. It’s really the kind of hidden perk you’d only find with a local.
Or if you’d rather keep things laid-back, you can combine the mountain views with a little gourmet twist on the with this Big Bear Lake jeep tour with light lunch. It’s part scenic ride, part storytelling session, and ends with a stylish pop-up picnic in a forest spot known mostly to locals. It’s perfect for a quiet lunch surrounded by fresh mountain air.
Quick Tips
- Check the weather. It can change fast in the mountains.
- Fill up on gas early. There aren’t many gas stations up in Big Bear, so top off before you start driving up the mountain roads.
- Take it slow on the roads. The mountain highways are beautiful but winding. Drive carefully and enjoy the views along the way.
More Fun Little Adventures Around Los Angeles
Echo Park Swan Boats
If you feel like swapping the city noise for something chill, I think paddling a swan boat around Echo Park Lake is a cute idea. It’s easy, affordable, and you can pick daytime or even go at night when the skyline’s all lit up. Nice way to just float, talk, and enjoy a break.
Ultimate LA Bike Tour
For something more active, you might like this full-day bike ride through West Hollywood, Beverly Hills, Santa Monica, and Venice. I like that it mixes cycling with little stories, celeb house sightings, and a stop at Greystone Mansion. It’s a fun way to cover a lot of ground without feeling rushed.
Universal Studios Hollywood: VIP Tour
If you’re into theme parks but hate standing in line all day, this VIP Universal pass could be worth it. You skip the lines, get a behind-the-scenes peek at real movie sets, and there’s even valet parking and a good meal thrown in. Not bad if you want to make the most of your day there.
Your Perfect LA Escape Awaits
Before you head out, keep a few things in mind to make the most of your LA day trips. Always check the weather, pack layers and sunscreen, and wear comfy shoes since you might hit a beach, a canyon, and a city street all in one day. If you’re driving, plan for traffic and parking fees, and start early when you can to avoid crowds.
It’s also worth keeping your energy up with some local bites. LA’s food scene is too good to skip! If you need ideas, I suggest browsing these famous Los Angeles foods for must-try eats along the way. And if you’re still building your plan, this list of things to do in Los Angeles can help round out your adventures. Enjoy exploring!

Table of Contents
Introduction
I woke up in my tiny Koreatown apartment, craving ocean air that didn’t smell like taco grease and Uber exhaust. By 7:15 a.m. I had a mug of cheap coffee, a half-charged phone, and enough gas to get somewhere—anywhere—before the 405 turned into a parking lot. These five day trips from los angeles saved my sanity over the past year; each one fits into a single Saturday, costs less than a Disneyland churro stand, and gives you bragging rights that don’t involve filtering selfies at the Hollywood sign.
Santa Barbara: ninety minutes to fake European bliss
The 101 north is a straight shot, but I still manage to miss the exit every time. Roll down the windows around Ventura and the air turns salty; by the time you hit Santa Barbara the temperature drops five degrees and your playlist suddenly feels more sophisticated. Park at East Beach lot ($2.25 per hour, card accepted) and walk the palm-lined path toward Stearns Wharf. I once saw a pelican steal a toddler’s sandwich here—equal parts horrifying and hilarious.
Almond croissants and hidden courtyards
I follow the same route each visit: croissant at Renaud’s (still warm, flaky enough to ruin your shirt), then a wander up State Street until the tilework of the old courthouse appears. If you’re building a bucket-list of single-day escapes, my Top Bucket List Travel Destinations You Can Explore in a Single Day guide rounds up global spots you can steal. I follow the same route each visit: croissant at Renaud’s (still warm, flaky enough to ruin your shirt), then a wander up State Street until the tilework of the old courthouse appears. Climb the tower—free, no line—and you’ll see red-tile roofs crammed between mountains and sea. Later I cut over to Anapamu Street, duck into the public library’s back garden, and pretend I’m in a Spanish novella for twenty minutes. No tour bus stops here; that’s the point.
Cheap wine without the side-eye
Santa Barbara’s Urban Wine Trail sounds bougie until you realize most tasting rooms pour for $10 and waive the fee if you buy a bottle. My go-to is Riverbench on Anacapa; their sparkling rosé tastes like strawberry Pop Rocks and the bartender lets you keep the glass. Dump the guilt, stash the glass in your trunk, and you’re back on the 101 before sunset traffic spawns.
Joshua Tree: where your phone gives up and you remember what stars look like
Two hours east and the city dissolves into wind farms, then boulder fields that feel like a Dr. Seuss fever dream. I always stop at the Joshua Tree Visitor Center for a map—even though the loop roads are basically a figure eight—because the ranger behind the counter gives free coffee refills to anyone carrying a reusable cup. If you ever flip the map to the desert north-east, my Unforgettable Day Trips from Las Vegas guide covers sun-to-snow routes in the same timeframe. Pro tip: bring the cup.
Hidden Valley loop before the crowds
I hit Hidden Valley Trail at sunrise; the parking lot has three cars max and the rocks glow pink. The loop is only one mile, but you’ll spend forty minutes photographing cacti and trying not to step on lizards. I once watched a guy propose here—she said yes, then immediately asked if there was cell service. (There isn’t.)
Keys View for the price of nothing
Drive another twenty minutes up the ridge and you’ll stare down the Coachella Valley from 5,185 feet. On clear winter days you can see the Salton Sea shimmering like a broken mirror. I sat on the stone wall until my fingers went numb, listening to nothing but wind and the occasional raven. That’s the real luxury—silence you don’t have to pay for.
Date shakes and gas-station art
Leave the park through the west entrance, pull into the funky strip of cabins that calls itself Joshua Tree town. Crossroads Café serves a date shake thick enough to stand a straw upright; I always add a shot of espresso because caffeine in the desert feels poetic. Next door, the thrift store has a wall of VHS tapes for a dollar each—buy one, even if you don’t own a VCR. It’s a souvenir that weighs nothing and sparks conversations.
Malibu: forty-five minutes to feel like a celebrity on a budget
Take the PCH north past Topanga and the cliffs drop into the ocean so fast your ears pop. I usually exit at Las Flores Canyon, park for free along the shoulder, and hike the paved path down to El Matador State Beach. The descent is steep enough to make your calves hate you, but the sea arches at the bottom photograph like a Greek island—no filter, no crowds before 10 a.m.
Sea caves and wet sneakers
Time the tide right (check the chart online) and you can duck into a cave that opens onto a hidden pocket of sand. I once found a message in a plastic bottle here: a kid’s drawing of a dinosaur and the words “be happy.” I left it there; the next person deserves the smile too.
Neptune’s Net: biker bar, surfer cafeteria, your lunch
Cross back over the highway and you’ll hit Neptune’s Net, all neon beer signs and Harley exhaust. Order the clam chowder bread bowl; it’s $12, tastes like salt and nostalgia, and the cashier doesn’t care if you show up in flip-flops or Ferragamo. Sit on the upper deck, watch the Pacific glitter, and try to count how many different languages you hear. I stopped at seven. Prefer palm trees to fog? Check my Ultimate San Francisco Day Trips guide for Nor-Cal ocean-to-redwood escapes too.
Big Bear Lake: two-and-a-half hours to fake winter when L.A. is still sweating
Climb the 330 through Running Springs and the temperature drops a degree every mile. I roll the windows down just to smell pine instead of brake dust. By the time the lake appears—frozen edges in January, glassy blue in July—I’ve already forgotten what freeway rage feels like.
Village Rim Trail for the lazy hiker
No skis? No problem. Park at the Discovery Center, grab a free map, and walk the Village Rim Trail. It’s mostly flat, hugs the shoreline, and delivers postcard views without the elevation guilt. I saw a bald eagle here last March; everyone else was taking selfies at the ski resort parking lot.
Coffee that doesn’t taste like campfire
Amangela’s sits above a bike shop that rents fat-tire cycles for snow. Their blueberry cornmeal muffin is the size of a softball and pairs perfectly with a honey-lavender latte. I always grab an extra muffin for the drive down—it’s gone before I hit the first switchback.
Alpine slide and alpine guilt
If you’re visiting summer-through-fall, the Alpine Slide at Magic Mountain is worth the $20. You ride a plastic sled down a concrete chute, wind in your face, lake expanding below. I screamed the entire way; the eight-year-old behind me did not. Humbling.
Solvang – Denmark without the jet-lag (2 hrs north-west)
Exit the 101 at Buellton, follow the smell of fresh waffles, and suddenly you’re in a Hans Christian Andersen pop-up book. Windmills spin, half-timbered houses lean at impossible angles, and every bakery pumps out almond-scented steam. I park on Copenhagen Drive—three free hours if you feed the meter quarters you found under the seat.
Kringle and Viking selfies
Mortensen’s Bakery has a tray of almond kringle that sells out by 11 a.m. I buy one still warm, eat it on the wooden bench outside, and pretend the calories don’t count on vacation days. Across the street, the giant red clog begs for a foot photo—obligatory, embrace the cliché.
Wine tasting that won’t bankrupt you
Walk two blocks south to Presidio Winery—tiny patio, string lights, laid-back bartender who pours four tastes for $8 and waves the fee if you post an Instagram story tagging them. Their sparkling brut is crisp enough to cut through kringle sugar; I left with two cans (yes, cans) because road-trip rules apply.
Quick comparison cheat-sheet
| Spot | Drive Time | Best Month | One Must-Eat | Parking Cash Needed |
| Santa Barbara | 90 min | Sept–May | Almond croissant | $8–15/day |
| Joshua Tree | 2 hrs | Oct–Apr | Date shake | $30 park fee |
| Malibu | 45 min | Year-round | Clam chowder bread | $10 shoulder |
| Big Bear | 2.5 hrs | Dec–Mar | Blueberry muffin | Free lots |
| Solvang | 2 hrs | Year-round | Almond kringle | Free 3 h |
Final reality check
You don’t need a private jet, a trust fund, or a three-day weekend. You need half a tank of gas, a Spotify playlist that doesn’t suck, and the guts to leave before sunrise. Every spot on this list I’ve done round-trip in under 12 hours, back home in time to shower, order Thai food, and sleep in my own bed. That’s the magic of day trips from los angeles: they feel like stolen time, not borrowed money.
